 SB 18

 SB 18 applies to local governments and requires local governments to contact, provide notice to, refer plans to, and
 consult with tribes prior to the adoption or amendment of a general plan or a specific plan, or the designation of
 open space. (Gov. Code §65352.3). Local governments should consult the Governor's Office of Planning and
 Research's "Tribal Consultation Guidelines," which can be found online at:
 https://www.opr.ca.gov/docs/09 14 05 Updated Guidelines 922.pdf.

 Some of SB 18's provisions include:

     1. Tribal Consultation: If a local government considers a proposal to adopt or amend a general plan or a
     specific plan, or to designate open space it is required to contact the appropriate tribes identified by the NAHC
     by requesting a "Tribal Consultation List.I' If a tribe, once contacted, requests consultation the local government
     must consult with the tribe on the plan proposal. A tribe has 90 days from the date of receipt of notification to
     request consultation unless a shorter timeframe has been agreed to by the tribe. (Gov. Code §65352.3
     (a)(2)).
     2. No Statutory Time Limit on SB 18 Tribal Consultation. There is no statutory time limit on SB 18 tribal consultation.
     3. Confidentiality: Consistent with the guidelines developed and adopted by the Office of Planning and
     Research pursuant to Gov. Code §65040.2, the city or county shall protect the confidentiality of the information
     concerning the specific ider:itity, location, character, and use of places, features and objects described in Public
     Resources Code §5097.9 and §5097.993 thal arewithin the city's or county's jurisdiction. (Gov. Code §65352.3
     (b)).
     4. Conclusion of SB 18 Tribal Consultation: Consultation should be concluded at the point in which:
              a. The parties to the consultation come to a mutual agreement concerning the appropriate measures
              for preservation or mitigation; or
              b. Either the local government or the tribe, acting in good faith and after reasonable effort, concludes
              that mutual agreement cannot be reached concerning the appropriate measures of preservation or
              mitigation. (Tribal Consultation Guidelines, Governor's Office of Planning and Research (2005) at p. 18).

 Agencies should be aware that neither AB 52 nor SB 18 precludes agencies from initiating tribal consultation with
 tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with their jurisdictions before the timeframes provided in AB 52 and
 SB 18. For that reason, we urge you to continue to re·quest Native American Tribal Contact Lists and "Sacred Lands
 File" searches from the NAHC. The request forms tan be found online at: http://nahc.ca.gov/resources/forms/.

•:NAHC Recommendations for Cultural Resources Assessments

 To adequately assess the existence and significance of tribal cultural resources and plan for avoidance, preservation
 in place, or barring both, mitigation of project.c.related impacts to tribal cultural resources, the NAHC recommends
 the following actions:

     1. Contact the appropriate regional California Historical Research Information System (CHRIS) Center
     (https://ohp.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=30331) for an archaeological records search. The records search will
     determine:
              a. If part or all of the APE has been previously surveyed for cultural resources.
              b. If any known cultural resources have already been recorded on or adjacent to the APE.
              c. If the probability is low, moderate, or high that cultural resources are located in the APE.
              d. If a survey is required to determine whether previously unrecorded cultural resources are present.

     2. If an archaeological inventory survey is required, the final stage is the preparation of a professional report
     detailing the findings and recommendations of the records search and field survey.
             a. The final report containing site forms, site significance, and mitigation measures should be submitted
             immediately to the planning department. All information regarding site locations, Native American
             human remains, and associated funerary objects should be in a separate confidential addendum and
             not be made available for public disclosure.

                                                         Page 4 of 5
             b. The final written report should be submitted within 3 months after work has been completed to the
             appropriate regional CHRIS center.

    3.   Contact the NAHC for:
            a. A Sacred Lands File search. Remember that tribes do not always record their sacred sites in the
            Sacred Lands File, nor are they required to do so. A Sacred Lands File search is not a substitute for
            consultation with tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the
            project's APE.
            b. A Native American Tribal ,Consultation List of appropriate tribes for consultation concerning the
            project site and to assist in planning for avoidance, preservation in place, or, failing both, mitigation
            measures.

    4. Remember that the lack of surface evidence of archaeological resources (including tribal cultural resources)
    does not preclude their subsurface existence.
           a. Lead agencies should include in their mitigation and monitoring reporting program plan provisions for
           the identification and evaluation of inadvertently discovered archaeological resources per Cal. Code
           Regs., tit. 14, § l 5064.5(f) (CEQA Guidelines§ l 5064.5(f)). In areas of identified archaeological sensitivity, a
           certified archaeologist and a culturally affiliated Native American with knowledge of cultural resources
           should monitor all ground-disturbing activities.
           b. Lead agencies should include in their mitigation and monitoring reporting program plans provisions
           for the disposition of recovered cultural items that are not burial associated in consultation with culturally
           affiliated Native Americans.
           c. Lead agencies should include in their mitigation and monitoring reporting program plans provisions
           for the treatment and disposition of inadvertently discovered Native American human remains. Health
           and Safety Code §7050.5, Public Resources Code §5097.98, and Cal. Code Regs., tit. 14, § 15064.5,
           subdivisions (d) and (e) (CEQA Guidelines§ 15064.5, subds. (d) and (e)) address the processes to be
           followed in the event of an inadvertent discovery of any Native American human remains and
           associated .grave goods in a location other than a dedicated cemetery.

From: Berkeley Waterfront Community Coalition
Re: Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry EIR Scoping Comments

Berkeley Waterfront Community Coalition is a nonprofit organization formed under the
auspices of Berkeley Partners for Parks, a 501(c)3 organization. Its founding members
are motivated by the diversity and range of stakeholders in the waterfront who
nevertheless have few channels of shared communication for supporting this unique
urban shoreline. BWCC’s mission is to develop projects that raise awareness of these
stakeholders, enhance a sense of community, and support the waterfront’s role in
providing value as affordable public access to blue- and greenspace amenities to the
region. Below we submit comments in response to City of Berkeley’s (COB) Notice of
Preparation and Scoping Meeting Environmental Impact Report for the Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry (NOP), dated April 18, 2025, in which COB is the lead agency
and the Water Emergency and Transportation Authority (WETA) is the responsible
agency under the proposal. In these comments, we also reference the City of Berkeley
Public Tidelands Area Project, aka the Waterfront Specific Plan (WSP), for commercial
redevelopment and recreation in the same area as the ferry project.

                                Overview of concerns

The Berkeley marina has long been a waterfront agora and mecca for city residents and
visitors seeking to use and enjoy its singular mixture of natural and human resources. It
draws a range of people of widely divergent economic means from Berkeley,
neighboring cities, and afar. All seek respite and recreation options in this local and
regional gem. Projects proposing major changes to the area’s physical and social
landscape must undergo rigorous debate about impacts, costs, and benefits affecting
both built structures and the cultural and human environment. In view of this, the EIR
must thoroughly and rigorously assess the physical, cultural and human environmental
impacts of the proposed new Berkeley pier and ferry service, expected to serve around
915 passengers departing per day (about 0.7% of the Bay Bridge vehicular traffic),
with its attendant facilities, including parking. In particular, the scope of the EIR must
characterize the individual and cumulative effects of a dual construction (pier plus ferry
facilities) on equitable access by the public, capital infrastructure and ongoing costs for
Berkeley/Alameda County residents, constriction of the marina’s limited parking
options, impacts on sustainable fishing and recreational boating, other environmental


                                                                                          1
impacts and overall utility to the people who use the marina. The scoping should
thoroughly consider alternatives to the proposed WETA ferry, including smaller ferries,
inside-marina docking, and no ferry at all. It must clearly evaluate the human and
environmental impacts of turning the marina into a transportation hub for a limited
population, versus reconstructing the pier to enable the Berkeley waterfront to serve as
a park unique to the Bay Area.

The outline of comments below is as follows:
   1. Impact on social equity and cultural resources
   2. Baseline conditions must be with pier and without ferry
   3. Impact on recreational and subsistence fishing
   4. Fish habitat
   5. Dredging for WETA ferry project is new dredging
   6. Characterization of alternatives
         a. Alternative 1: Ferry dock inside Marina
         b. Alternative 2: Smaller scale ferry
   7. Impact of tree removal
   8. Ferry parking management
   9. Bird nesting and feeding grounds
   10. Economic factors to contextualize project impact
   11. Compatibility of electrification and emergency service



   1. Impacts on social equity and cultural resources
The Berkeley Pier has long standing cultural significance for Berkeley. Since it was
closed to ferries in 1937, it has been a focal point for recreation and an important, low-
cost asset for many visitors. The Berkeley Fishing Memories Oral History Project
documents intergenerational and community connections to the outdoors as
experienced at the pier and waterfront by Berkleyans and frequent visitors. It reveals
how people have experienced and appreciated the recreational pier and waterfront as
“Berkeley’s backyard,” connoting a low-cost, welcoming, relaxed atmosphere where
children and adults enjoy the outdoors in a relatively safe space, for almost 90 years.
This use of this space is historical and current. For Berkeley, Alameda County, and
beyond, the pier and Berkeley Marina area are integral to low-cost public access to
bluespace. Among other data, the Kittleson parking study (p. 42) across lots in the
waterfront area underscores the socioeconomic diversity of current Berkeley waterfront
visitors. Forty-seven percent reported earning below the median household income for
Berkeley of $108,558
(https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/berkeleycitycalifornia/PST045224).




                                                                                             2
Science increasingly shows the positive impacts of regular bluespace exposure on
mental and physical health (Gascon et al. 2017, Pouso et al. 2021, Sturm and Cohen
2014, While et al. 2020). As the only urban shoreline in Berkeley, it provides a crucial,
inclusive center for public recreation, relaxation, interaction, and growth through
multiple educational and sport-related resources located at the Marina. Further, it
provides these benefits to historically underserved communities and low- and middle-
income users who have fewer means to travel to other coastal areas for shoreline
access.

While the NOP notes maintaining public space access as an objective, related COB and
WETA project documents and considerable COB Parks Department staff time has
focused on the needs of the proposed ferry service as the primary objective, with
recreation secondary. For example, during the course of WETA ferry project
negotiations, funds earmarked for waterfront and marina infrastructure have been
diverted to the ferry project at the expense of maintaining existing recreational
amenities. Further, basic, long-standing facilities central to the waterfront and marina’s
success as a bluespace public good – e.g. the failing seawall along the Bay Trail bike
path in front of the area’s two sailing clubs and docks, the recreational east dock in the
South Cove, and the watersports launch at Hs Lordship’s cove – have been allowed to
deteriorate and/or be shuttered. As of May 1, 2025, the COB has laid off its waterfront
security monitors, making recreational usage less safe and secure. These monitors
cost $100,000/year.

These points also illustrate overlaps in project scope between the ferry project and the
WSP. The spatial, policy and operational requirements of the ferry service impede
affordable recreational opportunities, as noted in the parking studies, as would a WSP
design focus to attract mainly ferry patrons. Data shows that riders in the WETA ferry
system tend to be high-income. Serving the high-income segment of population while
lessening services to others will transform the waterfront’s value as a cultural and
affordable public bluespace recreational resource into a transportation hub supporting
mainly a high-income ridership profile.




                                                                                           3
Figure 1: Image of east dock in South Sailing Basin, closed in February 2025. Cost of
repairs estimated at $250,000 are unfunded.

The EIR itself should consider that the proposed facility would be the only WETA ferry
terminal in the WETA system within a long-standing nature-based public park
where water-land recreation is an interconnected and highly-prized amenity. Compare
this concept to the locations of other WETA ferries:


   • Alameda/Oakland ferry – within Oakland’s Inner Harbor and shipping lanes for
       Port of Oakland, next to barge docks and naval ships
   •   Mare Island and Vallejo terminals – built in an unused location around Mare
       Island naval base and shipyard within the Mare Island Strait at mouth of Napa
       River. The land has long been dominated by housing development and the naval
       base.
   •   South San Francisco – by an industrial location within an existing Marina near
       the airport
   •   Richmond – site of former Ford factory and WWII shipbuilding site
   •   Alameda Seaplane Lagoon – within a decommissioned naval base
   •   Harbor Bay – the terminal serves the housing development and businesses
       around Bay Farm Island that closely abut the shoreline
   •   San Francisco terminals – at preexisting marine terminals and piers within
       industrial sites

At none of these ferry terminals is fishing, swimming, sailing, boating, and other
windsports a dominant activity on the water as they are at the Berkeley waterfront.
Those venues are already environmentally degraded: a large-scale ferry there does
not displace the pattern of park usage in “Berkeley’s backyard,” nor add substantially to
environmental damage. As currently conceived, the Berkeley pier-ferry plan attempts to


                                                                                         4
allow for recreation with what would be the only intentionally dual-use pier in the WETA
system. Unfortunately, many of the project elements listed are incompatible with
existing patterns of recreation.

The Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC) incorporates into its
goals and mission social equity in shoreline public access (BCDC, 2020). In October
2019 the agency amended the SF Bay Plan to incorporate issues of cultural diversity of
the waterfront and environmental justice considerations into its policymaking process
(Adapting 2019, BCDC 2019, Wasserman 2019). See in particular the BCDC SF Bay
Plan (https://bcdc.ca.gov/plans/sfbay_plan.html) under Major Proposals (4), Recreation:
Findings (b) (w), Recreation: Policies (1), (9), Public Access: Findings (b),
Environmental Justice and Social Equity: Findings (g), Policies (3).

EIR scoping input: BCDC policy requires protection of existing and future
recreational uses and consideration of social equity. As the proposed ferry is the
only terminal in the WETA system to be located in a primarily recreational park, the only
waterfront park in Berkeley, mandated as a recreational area by BCDC, the EIR must
rigorously assess the cumulative and distributional impacts of these overlapping WETA
ferry and WSP projects and their ultimate impact on the waterfront as a cultural
feature and affordable recreational resource, including loss of affordable
bluespace recreation, both existing and future. Specific items may include:


   • The EIR must acquire and present data on socioeconomic characteristics across
       all current and expected future visitation modes (via car, public transit, bike,
       walking) and recreational uses to the area and examine if the cumulative impacts
       of the proposed WETA ferry project and the Waterfront Specific Plan would
       “gentrify” the area such that affordable and inclusive access to green and
       bluespace recreation is impeded.
   •   In doing so, the EIR must identify increased costs and access barriers in terms
       of, for example, recreational space and amenities, recreational services, parking,
       access to the shoreline and water areas, and level and scope of commercial
       services.
   •   The EIR analysis must examine the consistency of the overall plans with BCDC
       policy on social equity in coastal recreation.
   •   The EIR must demonstrate that COB waterfront and park staff who maintain the
       area have the capacity and the directive to maintain low-cost recreational assets
       across areas located in the WSP and the ferry plan. As it stands, it is unclear
       that the COB has a sound plan to manage diverse recreational activities and
       public access for the life of the ferry project.




                                                                                           5
   2. Baseline comparison must be recreational demand at waterfront with
      pier and without ferry

City staff have indicated that the baseline for comparison is the status today of the
waterfront area and pier. However, COB closed the pier in 2015 after a long history of
popularity and high usage. Subsequent to closure, the city has made no new capital
investments to maintain walkways, seawalls, or adjacent parking lots around the
shoreline or pier. Around 2017, COB began negotiations with WETA for a ferry terminal,
reviving talks reflecting a 2008 proposal to place a WETA ferry terminal at the location.
Hs Lordships Restaurant closed in 2018 and remains derelict. D&E docks have been
removed. While there is still extensive usage of the waterfront despite 10 years of
minimal maintenance, the feasible baseline activity should be usage of a reopened
pier (to 2000’ or 3000’) on par with its length prior to closure, not baseline usage
after 10 years of the waterfront area falling into disrepair during COB-WETA
negotiations.

Research and reports indicate a large increase in public demand if the pier were
reopened and a basic functional facility maintained:
   •  Ken Jones, chronicler of pier fishing in California, states: “If a survey had been
      done over the past twenty-five years as to the most visited pier in the Bay Area,
      the winner undoubtedly would have been either the pier at Pacifica or this pier in
      Berkeley” and “For availability, transportation, ease of fishing, and facilities,
      Berkeley was hard to beat” (https://www.pierfishing.com/berkeley-pier/).
   •  Before its closure, Hs Lordships Restaurant was heavily used as an event space
      for large groups (e.g. school proms, Berkeley Public Schools Fund annual
      fundraiser, family reunions, etc.). Reviving the venue may see similar increases
      in demand, since few large event spaces at affordable prices exist in Berkeley.
   •  If the pier were reopened under the baseline condition of a somewhat shorter
      2000’ without the ferry, an economic valuation study by Antinori et al. (2025)
      predicts almost double the visitation rate for fishing over future expected visits to
      the shoreline along Seawall Drive.

COB 2021 states that replacement solely of the pier with a 2000-foot pier would cost
$26 million, and to 3000 feet, around $32-$44 million. City staff have indicated in public
meetings that COB’s share of the waterside costs alone for the pier/ferry project would
be approximately $26 million. Therefore, a 2000-foot reopened pier facility alone,
without a ferry, is a reasonable baseline, as it is the opportunity cost of the WETA/COB
pier/ferry project. Even as WETA and COB update all cost estimates to 2025 dollars
across all projects, as long as all costs scale relatively equally, this fact would remain.



                                                                                              6
EIR scoping input:

The EIR must take as a baseline the following conditions: Estimates of level and range
of usage for recreation and other non-ferry visitation should the original pier be
retrofitted/replaced and reopened to a length of 2000’, and with at least the following
baseline amenities repaired/reopened:
   •     Tenant activity for Hs Lordships location
   •     Street and walkway repair of Seawall Drive
   •     South Cove East Dock repaired
   •     D&E dock replaced

In doing so, the EIR must clarify whether the proposed ferry terminal and ~500’ pier with
~500 foot pier extension adequately accommodates historical, existing and future
expected recreational usage as compared to at least a 2000’ pier with the amenities
listed above.

   3. Impact on recreational and subsistence fishing

Before its closure in 2015, the pier was one of the most popular fishing venues in the
Bay Area. It hosted fishing derbies like the “mudfish” and kids’ fishing derbies. Closure
eliminated or displaced this activity to other piers. Fishers continue to visit the area
along the shoreline (which requires a license) as opposed to pier fishing, which does
not. According to a recent survey analysis from 2021 to 2023 (Antinori et al. 2025), 77%
of a random sample of shoreline anglers fished in Berkeley prior to COVID, implying a
long association with the area, and 61% said they prefer to fish in Berkeley in
comparison to other locations. In addition, 55% reported fishing for consumption needs.
Other locations like the piers in Pinole and Antioch are not substitutes for fishing at
Berkeley but appear to be complementary assets, with fishers traveling north and south
along I-80 (Antinori et al., 2025, p. 23) to these fishing spots.

Because pier fishing does not require a license, it is especially attractive to low-income
anglers. For example, Quimby et al. (2020) reported that in a study of pier fishing in
generally wealthy Santa Barbara, California, 88% reported annual household income
below the state median and 73% were non-white. Further, the study of Los Angeles pier
fishing by Stevenson et al. (2012) found that the majority identified as persons of color,
fished only from piers, and spoke English as a second language. Likewise, many
anglers who continue to fish the Berkeley shoreline are lower- to middle-income
(Antinori et al., 2025). This same study also projects an increase in angling visits should
the Berkeley pier reopen to even just a length of 2000’ without the ferry, of 70%, 88%
and 114% for low, middle, and high income anglers, respectively.


                                                                                          7
The environmental economics literature is replete with studies that estimate the value of
angling trips for recreational fishing. For example, Pendleton (2011) estimated a value
of $10 to $100/day (p. 156), and from $34-$536/ trip with charter boat fishing being
towards the high end (Pendleton and Rooke, 2006). California is second only to Florida
in percentage of population that participates in marine recreation (Pendleton and
Rooke, 2006). A recent study based on shoreline fishing at Berkeley puts the value at
$78 per trip, considering that the average shoreline fisher travels 24 miles one way from
their home to the Berkeley waterfront solely to fish. In springtime, sportfishing boats
and private boats go out into the Bay inside the Golden Gate bridge to fish for halibut.
According to a Barrientos et al. (2017) report on recreational benefits for the California
halibut recreational fishery, based on party/charter/private/rental fishing, Berkeley is the
highest valued port in northern California and most frequent port of embarkation for
halibut fishing for all of California.

Sources of Berkeley-specific fish reports and species caught off the pier near the
shoreline, along the existing (previously opened) pier, and from sportfishing boats
leaving out of the Berkeley marina include:

   1. BerkeleyMarina_baitntackle: Instagram posts on regular basis from the marina’s
      bait shop show catches from nearby Berkeley waterfront locations
   2. California Dawn sportfishing Facebook page:
      https://www.facebook.com/californiadawnsportfishing/
   3. Golden Eye 2000 sportfishing Facebook page:
      https://www.facebook.com/goldeneye2000sportfishing/

Although the WETA and WSP plans mention adding much-valued fishing amenities like
fish-cleaning stations and seats to the proposed pier extension, they include elements
with potential to reduce fishing as a recreational and subsistence activity. Yet, the
project makes practically no reference to nor includes data on fishing as a
potentially displaced activity with social equity consequences.

EIR scoping input for angling impact:
   •  Incorporate existing reports and studies on shoreline and pier fishing relevant to
      the Berkeley waterfront area to value changes in visitation rates for fishing and
      compare baseline condition of 2000’ pier without ferry and the dual use ~1000’
      pier with ferry and design-specific 400’ breakwater.
   •  The 400’ breakwater in the ferry plan is designed to service the ferry in sheet-pile
      cement design, which inhibits fish migration and spawning. The design
      encourages siltation and therefore requires additional dredging over time. The



                                                                                           8
       EIR should assess specifically the impact of the breakwater design and
       maintenance on fishing catch rates over the lifetime of the project.
   •   Examine potential safety risk and deterrent on fishing demand of crowding on a
       dual-use pier for the first 500’ of pier accommodating ferry passengers and
       recreational/subsistence fishers.
   •   Examine the impact of parking fees and access barriers in the WSP and ferry
       plan.
   •   Verify consistency of plan with BCDC policies on social equity with regard to
       fishing activity.
   •   Compare the baseline (at least) 2000’ pier which accesses deep water
       historically prized by fishers visiting the Berkeley pier to the ~500’ recreational
       pier extension to the proposed ferry pier and breakwater.
   •   Assess impacts on recreational/subsistence fishing of dredging along the pier
       and ferry route throughout project lifetime.
   •   Assess noise and traffic from ferry operations that would reduce catch rates and
       therefore the expected value of an angling trip to Berkeley.
   •   Expand analysis of the above to cover all seasons, not just a single point in time,
       to capture fishing effort which follows migration patterns of targeted fish species.
   •   Expand analysis to include a cumulative impact on above for the built-out ferry
       system beyond the proposed project outline.



   4. Fish habitat

While the comments in this section overlap with the section above, we attempt to isolate
and expand on impacts the biological resources themselves. The bay waters around
the pier prior to 2015 are known as spawning grounds for some fish species.
Fish populations are also migratory and seasonal, and interact with other parts of the
bay ecosystem. A number of plan elements could negatively affect fish habitat in the
area:
   •   Dredging to accommodate a large vessel alongside the pier close to shore
       (within 500’) plus initial construction and ongoing maintenance could interfere
       with all fish populations.
   •   An estimated 16 morning and 12 afternoon weekday crossings between Berkeley
       and San Francisco alone, plus 14 crossings on weekends and additional
       crossings for the Berkeley-Larkspur route, would create additional turbulence and
       noise, interfering with fish populations as well as angling (COB 2021 Feasibility
       Study).
   •   The original WETA plan called for a diesel ferry, while electric ferries were
       mentioned later in the process. Uncertainty remains whether an electric ferry


                                                                                          9
       would accommodate the natural conditions of the Berkeley pier, which
       experiences high winds and waves during much of the year.

EIR scoping input: EIR should assess impacts on all fish and marine species that are
part of the ecosystem in the path of the proposed WETA ferry with respect to:
   •    New and long-term maintenance dredging
   •    Siltation from a sheet pile breakwater that interferes with halibut and other fish
        spawning grounds and habitat
   •    Turbidity/turbulence and noise from the San Francisco, Larkspur and other
        routes in the plan
   •    Ship strikes
   •    Light pollution
   •    Diesel versus electric vessels

       5. Dredging for WETA ferry project is new dredging

The area proposed for the ferry route includes a federal navigation channel under the
Army Corps of Engineers. However, the channel is not dredged by the Corps, as it is
not considered a critical navigational location. Nor has it been dredged in possibly 50
years or more. The area proposed for the ferry dock has not been dredged recently
and should be considered new dredging.

The Berkeley Marina was partially dredged under a recent project permitted by the
Corps. The intended area is shown in the figure below. But it does not include the
channel proposed by the ferry route. Moreover, the area covered in the diagram was not
fully dredged.

                                                                                 12
       6. Characterization of alternatives

          a. Location alternatives must be adequately assessed

The only alternative examined by the WETA ferry plan is a site innermost in the
Berkeley Marina near an old slab of concrete that once served as a ferry dock (aka the
Old Ferry Pier). The last time this was used for a ferry was in 1989 by the Red and
White Fleet for about six months after the earthquake, after which it suspended service
due to lack of ridership. This location is not viable as an alternative, and acts a
“straw man” in the analysis as currently structured. During public meetings, the city
only offered as alternatives differences in breakwater design of the project.

Several feasible alternatives exist which have not been analyzed. One is the
previous D&E dock location near the Hornblowers docks and the Doubletree Hotel.
Another is the Hornblower docks themselves, in underused space. Third are docks
currently used by the Genentech and previously the Tidelines ferries, which closed
during the pandemic. The latter is a central location in the Marina and adds only two
minutes’ travel time to San Francisco, based on the Genentech ferry
departures/arrivals, excluding docking maneuver time.

In addition, an in-harbor dock reduces need for new dredging, and thus marginal
environmental impact, as the Marina undergoes maintenance dredging regardless. As
such it possibly reduces Berkeley’s cost of Marina maintenance because the needed
dredging costs could be shared over the years with WETA, and thus provide a more
viable economic pathway for ferry service.

EIR scoping input:
   •  EIR scoping should integrate the ferry project with the WSP and include
      examination of options to access a central in-Marina facility.
   •  Specifically, the EIR must assess, as a docking location alternative, a central
      location within the Marina, such as the previous D&E docks, Hornblower docks or
      the K docks.




                                                                                        13
Figure 5: Concrete slab inside Marina just above red traffic dot serviced old ferry, and is
innermost location. D&E dock location is much closer to entrance, out of sight in image
but on far right about halfway up. K dock extends from the harbormater’s office in center
of marina. The Hornblowers dock by the hotel on far right (not shown) in the marina.
Source:https://berkeleyca.gov/your-government/our-work/capital-projects/waterfront-
specific-plan

          b. Alternative scale of ferry should be included
Current ridership demand estimates for the WETA Berkeley-SF are 4000, using a 400-
passenger ferry, according to WETA business plan documents. Several indicators
suggest the WETA ferry may not reach this level of usage. Public transit demand is
down across the Bay Area systems including BART. About 60% of respondents in a
COB questionnaire said they would never use the ferry to commute. For leisure, 56%
said they’d never use it or use it less than 10 trips annually. There is a real danger
that the envisioned large-scale ferry with about 28 crossings per day would be
mainly empty. Stranded assets would pose a considerable cost to WETA and
Berkeley, as well as having serious environmental impacts.

A reasonable alternative of a smaller scale ferry service must be included in the EIR. A
smaller ferry would result in less cost, should demand predictions collapse. Smaller
scale service (and e.g. docking within the Marina) could reduce the financial burden on
Berkeley and at the same time fit demand patterns more accurately. However, smaller
scale ferries have not been considered in planning as alternatives.

EIR scoping input:


                                                                                        14
    • Examine costs and environmental impacts of an alternative smaller-scale electric
        ferry, say, for example, a 150-passenger ferry, as a feasible alternative to the
        current plan and assess the difference in environmental impact.
    •   Data on current usage by Genentech ferry and previous usage of Tidelines ferry
        ridership must be made available publicly for the report for a feasibility
        comparison of a small commuter ferry service operating in Berkeley.
    •   Data on the COB questionnaire must be included in the EIR and reconciled with
        WETA’s expansive ridership projections.

        7. Impact of tree removals

The Marina area faces the mouth of the Golden Gate, referred to as “The Slot” (see graphic
below). Existing large trees provide valuable wind relief to recreational visitors in the park for
land-based activities like picnics and park events. They also shelter half of the South Sailing
Basin, which supports children’s water sports training. Therefore, removing large trees should
be evaluated in terms of potentially decreasing the value of the park for recreational visitors, as
well as air quality and wildlife habitat. For example, close to the pier, large trees are the
roosting location for the resident wild turkeys. Hummingbirds nest in trees in Shorebird park.
The white-tailed kite and osprey hunt in Shorebird Park and south cove waters.

EIR scope input: Include analysis of tree removal impact on aesthetics, useability,
wind protection and bird and animal habitat in the area.

                               8. Ferry parking management

While this section overlaps with our first section on the waterfront as affordable
public access and cultural resource, here we emphasize the particular impact of
ferry patron parking on the Berkeley Marina as a major concern for equity,
recreational, and land use. The parking study introduces paid parking (currently free)
to recreational users. It forces them to park farther from Marina parks and shorelines.
For many, visits to the project area and waterfront are intimately tied to access via
private vehicle as well as public transportation. Sailors, windsurfers, wingers,
kayakers, fishers, families, guardians with children at the playgrounds, dog
walkers, picnickers and others, crucially, cannot pile considerable amounts of
gear, children, or animals aboard the 51 bus. Thus, public parking remains critical
to many who visit. A total of 16% in the Kittleson intercept survey said they
cancelled trips to the Marina because they could not find parking.




                                                                                                                                  16
Bus service to support ferry ridership is mentioned in the ferry parking study. However,
consultants noted the limited utility of buses for ferry patrons. The Kittleson study notes
in its case studies that AC Transit discontinued shuttle service to the Seaplane Lagoon
WETA terminal due to low ridership, and that AC transit service to the Harbor Bay ferry
terminal currently has few users.

It is unclear if and how Berkeley officials will fulfill their statutory obligation to keep ferry
riders from usurping recreational users’ parking. Past experience with Tidelines and
Genentech ferries shows that the city did not succeed in getting ferry patrons to
park outside of the South Cove recreational parking lots, raising doubt as to the
city’s motivation and/or ability to meet its BCDC obligations to preserve
recreational parking and access.

The recent parking study addendum also calls for expanding ferry patron parking to
Marina Boulevard and the Skates parking lot. This balloons the scope of the project
location as noted in the NOP. This proposal overlaps with the COB Waterfront Specific
Plan, which has not been completed, and is compiled independently from the pier/ferry
project even though the pier has historically been the central feature of the Berkeley
waterfront.

The 315-space Seawall Drive lot was closed in 2018 to deal with a homeless RV
encampment, and has been mostly closed ever since. This was a major lapse in the
city’s responsibility to maintain public access. Now the Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project intends to devote the entire Seawall Drive lot to ferry
parking. This will usurp Seawall Drive parking for people who fish or walk on the pier,
which is more than ironic, given that this expensive project was presented as a way to
reestablish the pier. Also usurped will be parking for new facilities at Hs Lordships
restaurant site, parking to serve the southern Shorebird Cove picnic sites, and the
boardsailing and swimming launch at Hs Lordships Cove, to say nothing of overflow
parking for the heavily impacted South Cove parking lots.

EIR scoping questions:

   • Include analysis of what the city has done in the past when recreational parking
       was displaced by the Genentech and Tidelines ferry and plans for future, more
       effective enforcement capacity if large-scale ferry service is implemented.
   •   Expand project location to include all locations noted in the addendum to the
       parking study.




                                                                                                17
   • Examine cumulative and distributional impacts of parking from the WSP and the
      pier/ferry project on the public’s recreational use, affordable access, and the
      extant legal land use designations.




Figure 7: South Cove west parking lot on Saturday, May 10, 2025 at 1pm, with east lot
in background. Both are almost entirely used by recreational visitors. Paving the lot as
planned will significantly reduce the number of parking spaces. The Kittleson ferry
parking study attempts to plan for ferry parking in conjunction with the WSP. (Photo: C.
Antinori)

      9. Bird nesting and feeding grounds

The waterfront area is home to many birds in Cesar Chavez Park
(https://ebird.org/hotspot/L285281/bird-list) and the Sylvia McLaughlin State Park, part
of the Eastshore State Park system. Resident bird populations include ospreys who
feed in nearby waters.

EIR scoping input: The cumulative impacts of the WSP and the ferry project need to
take into account increased noise, increased traffic, tree removal, new and maintenance
dredging, ferry operations, and reconfiguration of parking patterns on bird habitat, over
the course of migratory and seasonal cycles rather than at one point in time. In doing
so, it should:


   • Document all bird species in area, migratory and resident

                                                                                        18
   • Use eBird "hotspots" and other sources to name the birds documented in the
       area, potentially up to to 200 species. (https://ebird.org/hotspots)
   •   Consider the loss of trees at Shorebird Park that support hummingbirds (see
       section 7)
   •   Incorporate information that the burrowing owl is currently under consideration to
       be added to the Endangered Species list of the State of California
       (https://wildlife.ca.gov/News/Archive/cdfw-seeks-public-comment-related-to-
       western-burrowing-owl)
   •   Include bird species identified at the project location that are among the CA
       Species of Special Concern and Fully Protected Species. This includes the
       White-Tailed Kite and osprey (https://wildlife.ca.gov/Conservation/SSC/Birds)

       10. Clarify economic factors to contextualize project feasibility

As BCDC considers environmental impacts overall and weighs any opportunity cost for
not building the large-scale WETA ferry, realistic information should be provided about
those opportunity costs. WETA documents offer no predictions, nor conjectures, of
secondary economic benefits for Berkeley. Consultant reports suggest minimal
economic benefits. The Keyser Marston report suggests very modest contributions to
the Marina Fund which may generate only up to 10% more of any revenues the city
receives from food and beverage consumer spending (Keyser Marston, 2021, pp. 8-9).
The report extends only aspirational comments, e.g. “It is hoped that a large-scale
ferry with weekend service will attract an additional hotel” (Keyser Marston, p. 9).
The WETA ferry terminal at Jack London Square, Oakland, has failed to prevent a
large vacancy rate in commercial rental space. Oakland’s Waterfront Hotel which
closed in January 2025 had 145 rooms, just steps away from this terminal.

EIR scoping should include: Currently available estimates of the secondary economic
benefits so that reviewers may weigh the proposed project against its environmental
and human costs. The scoping should compare this against the baseline of 2000’ pier
without ferry.

       11. Compatibility of electrification and emergency service

The waterfront area is land filled for recreational purposes. As fill, the waterfront area
servicing the dock may not be stable in an earthquake. The ferry dock is described as
serving an electric ferry if feasible. In such a case, an electrification facility to serve
electric zero-emission ferry vessels may not withstand natural disasters such as
earthquakes, tsunamis or violent storms.



                                                                                              19
Storms also come from north and south throughout the year, making navigation in “The
Slot” through the Golden Gate (see above) more challenging. Any final recharging
station and breakwater design compatible with supporting electric ferry service year-
round and in emergencies should be confirmed within the EIR. With this information,
environmental impacts noted above (e.g. dredging, aesthetics, recreation, habitat) can
be more clearly assessed.

EIR scoping input:
   •  To properly understand the environmental impact of the above, the EIR must
      provide specifications on infrastructure to serve an electric ferry vessel in an
      emergency. If it cannot, then it must delete references to emergency response in
      the scope of the project.
   •  If it specifies electrification infrastructure to withstand natural disasters, then it
      should specify whether the ferry service will be able to handle emergency
      vehicles or just personnel. Include technical specifications of breakwater design
      to support operations year-round and in emergencies.

RE: Draft EIR Scoping Comments for Berkeley Pier Ferry Project

Dear Liza McNulty,

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments related to the scoping of environmental issues to be
included in the EIR for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry. We were very happy to see that the
ferry fleet will be all electric. Zero emissions will reduce some direct impacts to nearby wildlife while
helping reduce climate impacts.

Golden Gate Bird Alliance is a non-profit organization based in Berkeley whose mission is to inspire
people to protect Bay Area birds and our shared natural environment. For over 100 years we have been a
leader in Bay Area wildlife conservation, protecting birds and their habitats. Our 7,000 Bay Area
members and supporters envision a world where birds, wildlife, and all people flourish together.

We have reviewed the Notice of Preparation for the EIR, and request that the following issues be
specifically addressed in the EIR:

    •   Impacts of increased boat traffic to waterbirds that use the waters adjacent and just offshore of the
        proposed ferry terminal, especially during winter when waterbirds are most abundant in the area.
        Additionally, spring and fall periods should be studied for species present during these critical
        migration periods. The offshore areas are critical overwintering habitat for many species of ducks,
        grebes, pelicans, terns, gulls, and other waterbirds.

    •   Wave impacts from the proposed ferry activities on adjacent shorelines that support shorebirds
        and mudflat habitats, including any potential interactions of wave impacts and future sea-level rise
        on these habitats.

    •   Direct impacts of the proposed dock, including shading on subtidal habitats.
    •   Direct impacts of dredging, including the proposed frequency of dredging, as well as the
        beneficial reuse of dredged material within the Bay.

    •   Impacts to existing bird and wildlife habitat adjacent to the pier and parking area (e.g., tree
        removal or other impacts to these areas).

    •   Opportunities to use native plantings throughout the project.

    •   Increased contaminant runoff from the parking lots associated with the ferry terminal.

Additionally, although the Monterey Cypresses in the existing parking area are not native to the Bay Area
specifically, they are native to California and commonly used in native landscaping efforts. Despite being
mature to senescent and perhaps not the most diverse vegetation type, these trees have long provided
shelter for species such as Black-crowned Night-Herons and Pygmy Nuthatches. We hope the EIR's
potential project alternatives will look at the possibility of adding additional terrestrial bird and wildlife
habitat, using native plants to support greater biodiversity of birds and insects.

Thank you for your consideration of these scoping elements in the environmental review process. Please
do not hesitate to reach out for clarification or if we can provide additional details.

Sincerely,




Glenn Phillips
Executive Director

Dear Lisa McNulty,

We are frequent swimmers at the Berkeley Marina and members of the QT Selkies Gay
for the Bay a community of nearly 225 individuals who swim throughout the Bay Area,
including locations in Berkeley, Oakland, Richmond, Pinole, Albany, Alameda, and San
Francisco.

We've been following the city's proposal to redevelop the marina to accommodate ferry
service, but it has been challenging due to the lack of accessible public information. I
am writing today to express our concerns about this development and lay out how our
swimmers currently use the marina.

Swimmers require three essential things: a safe entry point, clean water to swim in, and
convenient parking. Our community typically enters the water near the seawall adjacent
to the former Hs Lordships restaurant. This location is vital, especially during low tides
when the sailing basin becomes too shallow for safe swimming and launching
conditions that occur roughly half the time. And seeing as this location is only one of two
in the East Bay that can be accessed regardless of tide we are very attached to its
existence. We, along with other waterfront users like anglers, walkers, paddlers, and
windsurfers, rely on parking along the seawall. We are concerned that ferry riders will
dominate these spaces.

We've been informed by other swimmers who attended the March PRWC meeting that
they were troubled by the city's claim that parking would remain sufficient for all users.
The data backing this assertion appears selectively chosen. Specifically, page 22 of the
report reveals that parking surveys were conducted at 10am and 8pm times not
reflective of peak use (typically 2pm 4pm) and focused more on overnight vehicle
stays than daytime activity.

The assumption that all marina parking is interchangeable overlooks practical realities.
After a cold swim, it's unreasonable to expect individuals to walk half a mile or more
across the marina to reach distant lots.

We're deeply concerned that increased commercialization of the marina could
reduce access to free, low-barrier recreational opportunities that draw an
exceptionally diverse group of users. We believe the current planning is being
guided by flawed data and that local residents and regular recreational users
have not been adequately included in the process.
We urge the BCDC to call on the city to conduct a more thorough and accurate
analysis of parking and waterfront access, and to commit to protecting the public
amenities that make the Berkeley Marina such a vital recreational space.

Thank you for your commitment to equitable access to the Bay for all.

Sincerely,
Robin Mangini, MPH
Co-Admin of the QT Selkies Gay for the Bay

RE: Scoping Comments on the Notice of Preparation for the Berkeley Waterfront
Specific Plan and Ferry Project EIR



Dear Ms. McNulty,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Notice of Preparation (NOP)
for the Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Berkeley Waterfront Specific Plan and
Berkeley Ferry Project. For over sixty years Save The Bay has worked to protect and
restore San Francisco Bay for people and wildlife, including stopping the City of
Berkeley's plan to fill another two square miles of San Francisco Bay. These comments
are offered to assist the City of Berkeley as the lead CEQA agency to prepare a legally
adequate EIR that informs public discussion on the best project alternative that avoids
significant environmental impacts.

The City of Berkeley proposes to develop a ferry terminal and restore the historic
Berkeley Pier to meet regional transit needs and enhance public access to the
waterfront. This project EIR must include full evaluation of the project's environmental
impacts, as well as an evaluation of all legally required alternatives, in accordance with
the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). We highlight below a few of the many
considerations the EIR must address.

The project's proximity to three major public open spaces-Shorebird Park, Adventure
Playground, and McLaughlin Eastshore State Park- requires detailed focus on impacts
to recreation and transportation. Areas of the Bay that have been filled for recreational
purposes should remain in that use and not be converted for commercial development,
consistent with provisions of the McAteer-Petris Act and regulations of the San
Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC). Save The Bay and
its founders (including Sylvia McLaughlin for whom Eastshore State Park is named)
supported the placement of fill in the Bay in Berkeley only for recreational purposes, as
consistent with BCDC's statute.
                                SAVE~BAY
BCDC's 1967 permit to fill an area of the bay and expand Berkeley marina stated that
the purpose of the fill was to " ... permanently establish public access and recreational
use for a sizable part of the Berkeley shoreline." BCDC issued the permit relying on the
statements of city officials including Sylvia McLaughlin, who wrote that "Berkeley's
portion of the shoreline of San Francisco Bay should be reserved exclusively for public
recreation and its related public uses." Berkeley citizens also approved a 1968
referendum, titled the "Berkeley Public Parks and Open Space Preservation Ordinance,"
establishing their commitment to preservation of parks and open space, codified as
Ordinance No. 5785-N. S. The definition of parks and open space protected by that
ordinance clearly applies to the areas that would be altered by the project described in
this Notice of Preparation.

The EIR should also address whether the project and any of its alternatives are
consistent with BCDC's adopted recreational policies and maps that protect existing
recreational amenities including the bay fill in the project area and the Berkeley Marina,
which is designated as a waterfront park priority use area in BCDC's Bay Plan. BCDC's
Recreational Policy 9 states:


       "Ferry terminals may be allowed in waterfront park priority use areas and
       marinas and near fishing piers and launching lanes, provided the
       development and operations of the ferry facilities do not interfere with
       current or future park and recreational uses, and navigational safety can
       be assured. Terminal configuration and operation should not disrupt
       continuous shoreline access. Facilities provided for park and marina
       patrons, such as parking, should not be usurped by ferry patrons. Shared
       parking arrangements should be provided to minimize the amount of
       shoreline area needed for parking." (San Francisco Bay Plan, Policy 9)

The EIR should evaluate whether the proposed project and any of its alternatives can
be consistent with that ordinance, BCDC's permit, and other local, state and federal
laws and regulations.

The Berkeley Waterfront receives up to 300,000 visits per year and includes many
shoreline access points in the Bay Area. Any effects on these public resources or on
shoreline recreational access will negatively impact the local population and the public
throughout the region. With rising temperatures due to climate change, demand for
access to McLaughlin Eastshore State Park's shoreline recreation areas will continue to
increase. The EIR must analyze how the project's proposed infrastructure to support
ferry service - terminal facilities, parking, shoreside infrastructure for ferry boats, and
more - that may provide benefits to some individuals who ride the ferry, will create
negative impacts on the many park users who do not use that service. Those impacts
                               SAVE~BAY
include increased traffic through park areas, barriers to shoreline access, disruption of
views, and more.

Given all of the significant potential impacts to people and wildlife, including those
explicitly protected by local, state and federal laws and regulations, the EIR should
evaluate alternatives that do not involve the use and alteration of land reserved for
recreational purposes. Filled land in the Bay that pre-dates the establishment of BCDC
provides the City of Berkeley broader discretion to apply uses consistent with the Public
Trust Doctrine but not restricted by BCDC permits. Berkeley's marina basin already
provides about 1,000 recreational boat slips and additional areas for charter boats
including the Genentech ferry and Hornblower charters. This EIR should include
alternatives that consider this and other sites that require little or no new filling and
dredging of the Bay, elimination of current recreational parking and other impacts.

The project's location on the Bay shoreline, near sensitive wildlife and habitat, also
necessitates the study of impacts and alternatives that protect water quality and
pollution impacts on aquatic and terrestrial species and on people who use the area,
including swimmers, windsurfers, kayakers, sailors and others. The EIR should assess
impacts from and alternatives to construction activities on shore and in the Bay,
including dredging, placement of fill and installation of infrastructure. Changes to ground
permeability that affect stormwater runoff pollution should also be assessed and the EIR
should identify how alternatives will avoid these impacts and mitigate any impacts that
are unavoidable.


Save The Bay is deeply invested in helping Bay Area communities build resilience in the
face of climate change. This EIR must evaluate the project's impact on local air quality
and greenhouse gas emissions and should be designed for long-term adaptation to sea
level rise, including incorporation of nature-based solutions along the shoreline to
protecting infrastructure and ecological resources from flooding. The project should
avoid shoreline development that will necessitate hard armoring of the shoreline that
risks additional negative environmental impacts including erosion and loss of public
access in the future. Alternatives should prioritize ways to work with nature, rather than
against it, in equipping shoreline development to withstand long-term sea level rise.

In summary, the EIR must evaluate a full range of alternatives, including the least
environmentally damaging feasible alternative. Alternatives should aim to avoid impacts
to public trust resources, water quality, greenhouse gas emissions, and shoreline
resilience, and minimize any unavoidable significant impacts. We look forward to
continued engagement in the environmental review process and thank you for
considering our comments.

Sincerely,
                     SAVE!BAY



David Lewis
Executive Director

       Re: Comments on Notice of Preparation of EIR for Berkeley Ferry

Dear Ms. McNulty:

       The Sierra Club California State Parks Committee and Bay Alive Committee provide the
following comments regarding the issues and matters that the Berkeley Ferry EIR should address. You
have already received comments from the San Francisco Bay Chapter Northern Alameda Group. These
comments are in addition to those comments.

        The Sierra Club is deeply concerned about the future health of the San Francisco Bay, its
ecosystems that provide services to us all, and the wildlife that the Bay supports. We are committed to
the protection and enhancement of our Bay's ecosystems and habitats. As sea levels rise and
atmospheric river storms become more prevalent, the Berkeley shoreline becomes more vulnerable to
wave run-up and flooding. In addition, the Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC)
recently passed the Regional Shoreline Adaption Plan (RSAP) Guidelines which will require cities like
Berkeley to prepare their own Subregional SAP in compliance with the requirements of the BCDC
RSAP Guidelines in order to deal with the projected rise responsibly and constructively in Bay waters.

        The access road from the urban area of Berkeley to the Berkeley Marina where the ferry terminal
would be constructed cuts through portions of the McLaughlin Eastshore State Park (MESP). The access
road is adjacent to the Conservation area in the Berkeley Meadow of the MESP. The ferry terminal and
other proposed infrastructure changes would also be adjacent to the protected waters of the South Basin
Cove of the MESP. The water areas around the proposed terminal site also include the North Basin
Cove of the MESP. Under the MESP general plan the North Basin Cove has special seasonal and other
protections for rafting and migrating birds. The proposed ferry may have impacts on bird species in
those waters.
Sierra Club to Berkeley                             1
Re: Berkeley Ferry Terminal
Comments on the NOP
2025-05-19
       In light of these physical constraints, our review of the proposed ferry terminal and mixed-use
development at the Berkeley marina raises substantial environmental and infrastructural concerns.


Construction Impacts and BCDC RSAP Guidelines

         The construction of appropriate nature-based shoreline infrastructure, to minimize impacts, may
require additional setbacks. The environmental impacts of construction and operation of a ferry
terminal, parking lot, and access road should be analyzed and either minimized or mitigated. BCDC's
RSAP guidelines will undoubtedly also influence how this shoreline infrastructure should address sea
level rise and utilize Natural and Nature Based solutions (NNBS) as part of the RSAP. In addition, the
proposed development site is on Bay fill and as sea levels rise, groundwater is also expected to rise.
These Bay fill soils are prone to liquefaction in the event of earthquakes which we all know are
inevitable in the Bay Area. This potential liquification should be addressed.


Issues Concerning Alternative Development Sites

        The EIR must analyze reasonable alternatives. An alternative that is not reasonable and that
should not be used is for a ferry terminal at the Albany Golden Gate Fields racetrack site. The track is
now closed. The Sierra Club has called for the entire Golden Gate Fields site to be acquired and added
to the MESP. The Club has also stated that after acquisition over time, the site should be restored to its
original wetland and marsh that covered most of the site in the early 1900' s before it was filled for the
track. This restoration would further BCDC's goals ofrestoring and increasing wetlands and marsh in
the Bay thus creating a resilient shoreline using NNBS which is one of the primary goals of the BCDC
RSAP.


Bay Fill and Groundwater Rise

     The proposed ferry includes parking and other structures that are situated on bay fill, which is prone
to liquefaction in seismic events. Rising sea levels will also elevate groundwater levels, further
destabilizing these soils. This poses significant risks for the construction and long-term viability of the
site for a ferry terminal and need to be fully analyzed in the EIR.



Environmental Impact of Ferry Terminal

    The construction and operation of the ferry terminal could detrimentally impact nearby sensitive
habitats especially the Conservation area on the Berkeley Meadow in the MESP, and the North and
South Basins. Increased boat wakes could harm migratory birds and other aquatic species. If the ferries
are not electric, then ferry diesel emissions pose a pollution risk. A Water Emergency Transit Authority
(WETA) study demonstrated that ferries create dead zones for waterfowl in the ferry wake zone thus
significantly impacting those species. Mitigations such as slow speed requirements around recognized

Sierra Club to Berkeley                              2
Re: Berkeley Ferry Terminal
Comments on the NOP
2025-05-19
rafting duck locations should be considered as mitigation requirements. Comprehensive mitigation
strategies must be developed and evaluated to minimize these environmental impacts. The potential
impacts on bird species protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty must be analyzed. We refer you to
the attached addendum, Takegawa, John, Effects ofFerry Traffic on Migratory Wasterbirds in the San
Francisco Bay. (Exhibit A)



Potential for private ferries

    We also continue to be extremely concerned about WETA's future plans to consider allowing
private ferries at various terminals. The project description includes the possible addition of special
event service. It does not specifically forbid private vehicles. If private ferries (that are both scheduled
and unscheduled) and water taxis (similar to calling an Uber or Lyft water taxi) are allowed to use the
dock and terminal facility, this presents a significant problem It is important to monitor and enforce
speed restrictions of boats as well as to minimize the number of boats through the refuge. It has been
clearly demonstrated that it is difficult or impossible to do daily enforcement of speed restrictions of
private ferries or water taxis.
    Additional boats, especially private ferries, and water taxis that are not obeying the speed
restrictions, would cause more environmental and safety concerns including more wake waves, potential
impacts on rowers and paddlers in non-motorized watercraft, shoreline erosion, and impacts on birds and
other aquatic species.


Air Quality

Evaluate the impact of ferry diesel emissions on recreational users of the waterway as well as adjacent
shoreline communities. If the project plan includes backup power using diesel fuel, include those
emissions in the analysis.


Artificial Light at Night (ALAN)

Due to proximity to MESP and protected waters, night lights from the terminal and parking areas will be
harmful to birds and other wildlife in the nearby MESP. ALAN interferes with bird reproduction,
feeding and migration. Night foraging creatures will not be able to forage if lights are on at night and
shine on the water. The EIR must evaluate approaches to and require minimizing ALAN and lighting
and use of the site after sundown.


Noise

        The EIR must evaluate the maximum decibel of the ferries and of other equipment at the project
site and their impact on birds and other wildlife. Ensure that there are no private boats using the dock,
especially at night, such as party boats or special event boats. Evaluate the impact of construction period
Sierra Club to Berkeley                               3
Re: Berkeley Ferry Terminal
Comments on the NOP
2025-05-19
and noise including pile driving and length of construction time on adjoining habitat and species.
Considering the disruption and noise during the construction period, will a significant area of this
valuable wildlife habitat be no longer viable for wildlife that now consider it home?


Bird Safe Design

        Bird-safe design principles are crucial for protecting avian populations, particularly in areas
adjacent to wildlife refuges. These principles aim to prevent bird collisions with structures, which is a
significant threat to bird safety. Structures such as buildings, windows, and other man-made objects
often pose hazards to birds, leading to injuries or fatalities. Implementing bird-safe designs is essential
to minimize these risks and promote a safe environment for birds, especially in areas with high bird
activity.

        The Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 (16 U.S.C. 703-712) provides that it is unlawful to
pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, possess, sell, purchase, barter, import, export, or transport any migratory
bird, or any part, nest, or egg or any such bird, unless authorized under a permit issued by the Secretary
of the Interior. Since the areas in the MESP and in and around the proposed terminal site are used by
migratory birds, the impact of the ferry on migratory birds must be analyzed.


Geology, Soils, and Seismicity

        The EIR must include information on the soils at the site as well as along the only access road
that gives access to the site. Soil settlement along the two mile access road indicates unstable soils.


Hazards and Hazardous Materials

        Recent investigations have revealed that there are fill areas on the Albany, Berkeley, and
Richmond shorelines that have toxic and hazardous materials. A thorough review of historical and
current environmental data is necessary to assess potential contamination risks.



Utilities and Service Systems

       The EIR must analyze the life service of existing utilities and storm water/wastewater systems.
Rising groundwater may be poised to inundate portions of the buried utilities off site that are serving the
site.


Transportation Issues from Increased Gas Powered Automobiles
       The ferry terminal will result in greater automobile use to and from the ferry terminal. The
increase in such especially from gas powered automobiles in terms of air quality and impacts from
cadmium and other toxic materials found in automobile tires must be analyzed, especially as to impacts
Sierra Club to Berkeley                              4

on wildlife and habitat in the MESP. Therefore, the EIR should analyze how the impact of gas powered
cars can be mitigated through increased bus service and bicycle access to the ferry terminal. See the
attached March 27, 2025 letter from the Club's Northern Alameda Group to the City of Berkeley.
(Exhibit B)

EFFECTS OF FERRY TRAFFIC ON MIGRATORY WATERBIRDS IN THE SAN FRANCISCO BAY

Commuter ferry routes cross valuable subtidal and intertidal habitats in the San Francisco Bay estuary
that support a wealth of natural resources, including large numbers of migratory waterbirds during the
winter. When new routes were proposed for the region under a new transit authority in 1999, we initiated
studies to evaluate the ecological effects of commuter ferries on rafting waterbirds. The main objectives
were to: 1) conduct on-board ferry surveys to assess species-specific buffer distances; 2) examine
waterbird avoidance of watercraft in land-based surveys at selected areas; and 3) document distribution of
waterbirds along ferry routes with aerial surveys.

On-board ferry surveys were used to determine how waterbirds responded behaviorally to the passage of a
commuter ferry. Observers recorded the behavioral response (fly, dive, swim, alert posture) of waterbirds
and their distance from the ferry. Surf scoters (Melanittaperspicillata), lesser and greater scaup (Aythya
affinis and A. marila), and western and Clark's grebes (Aechmophorus occidentalis and A. clarkii) were
the most abundant species found across all ferry routes, with diving ducks representing the most
abundant guild. Behavior response distances ranged from 50-500 m for grebes, 30-900 m for scoters, and
60-500 m for scaup. Most waterbirds showed a behavior response within 300 m, and we used that
distance to estimate the zone within which birds were affected. In addition, we used GPS tracking to
determine that variation in the path of the ferries was usually 200 m. Thus, we calculated a total effect
area along a ferry route from their sum or a distance of 500 m. Affected areas ranged from 2-44 to 75.75
krn2 and included 0.07-14.26 krn2 of shoals preferred for foraging ( <4 m deep).

We studied the duration of disturbance of a ferry transit from land-based surveys. At selected sites, we
recorded numbers and behavior of waterbirds before and after transit. Scaup densities declined after ferry
transit along the Vallejo and Alameda Harbor Bay route, and scoters decreased after passage of the
Larkspur ferry. However, patterns were not consistent, probably because birds were responding to several
factors such as time-of-day, weather, and other disturbances. When we compared weekday to weekend
surveys, we found more waterbirds along routes during the weekdays despite more frequent ferry traffic.

Aerial surveys indicated that diving ducks accounted for 85% of open water birds, dominated by scaup
and scoter (90%). Numbers were highest during Nov-Dec in the North Bay, consistent in the central Bay,
and lowest in the South Bay. While new commuter ferries may be beneficial at reducing vehicle traffic,
they will have an effect on waterbird populations. Although they do not eliminate open water habitats,
they may preclude use of it by waterbirds. Thus, our study indicated that effects on waterbirds should be
considered when planning new transit routes or increasing their frequency, especially in shoal areas used
for foraging.

Dear Mayor and Council,

The Sierra Club North Alameda County Group strongly encourages Berkeley to take a
more holistic, non-single occupancy vehicle-centric approach to planning for future ferry
passenger capacity at the Berkeley Marina. Taking steps to meaningfully promote
transportation alternatives is a key step towards the city meeting its climate and
emissions goals, as well as encouraging more equitable and less environmentally
impactful transportation options for commuters and visitors.

The strategies put forth in the Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Parking and TOM
Plan will only serve to encourage people to drive to the Berkeley Marina when
accessing the new ferry service. Increasing parking, formalizing overflow parking
locations, and improving wayfinding to and from these overflow lots and the ferry
terminal are ultimately strategies to make driving easier, which will invariably lead to
more driving. The phenomenon of induced demand is well-studied in transportation
demand management, and its results are predictable. In addition, the cost-effectiveness
of investments in bus and rail transit compared to trips by ferry that are more costly per
rider strongly indicate that the City should avoid discretionary local investments
supporting parking, while receiving grants and other resources developed by WETA.

Instead, we believe that the City of Berkeley should be prioritizing improvements to
alternate modes of travel to and from the Marina and new ferry terminal, which aligns
more closely with the city's own goals. These include:

   -     Improved bicycle infrastructure and connections: Protected bike lanes along
         University Ave, safer and more direct connections from West Berkeley to the
         Marina, and ample bicycle parking in close proximity to the terminal, in addition to
