       Re: Comments on Notice of Preparation of EIR for Berkeley Ferry

Dear Ms. McNulty:

      The Sustainability, Parks, Recycling, and Wildlife Legal Defense Fund (SPRAWLDEF)
provide the following comments regarding the issues and matters that the Berkeley Ferry EIR
should address.

      SPRAWLDEF is deeply concerned about the future health of the San Francisco Bay, its
ecosystems that provide services to us all, and the wildlife that the Bay supports. We are committed
to the protection and enhancement of our Bay's ecosystems and habitats. As sea levels rise and
atmospheric river storms become more prevalent, the Berkeley shoreline becomes more vulnerable
to wave run-up and flooding. In addition, the Bay Conservation and Development Commission
(BCDC) recently passed the Regional Shoreline Adaption Plan (RSAP) Guidelines which will
require cities like Berkeley to prepare their own Subregional SAP in compliance with the
requirements of the BCDC RSAP Guidelines in order to deal with the projected rise responsibly
and constructively in Bay waters.

      The access road from the urban area of Berkeley to the Berkeley Marina where the ferry
terminal would be constructed cuts through portions of the McLaughlin Eastshore State Park
(MESP). The access road is adjacent to the Conservation area in the Berkeley Meadow of the
MESP. The ferry terminal and other proposed infrastructure changes would also be adjacent to the
protected waters of the South Basin Cove of the MESP. The water areas around the proposed
terminal site also include the North Basin Cove of the MESP. Under the MESP general plan the
                                                      1

SPRAWLDEF to Berkeley

Re: Berkeley Ferry NOP, 2025-05-19
North Basin Cove has special seasonal and other protections for rafting and migrating birds. The
proposed ferry may have impacts on bird species in those waters.

      In light of these physical constraints, our review of the proposed ferry terminal and mixed-
use development at the Berkeley marina raises substantial environmental and infrastructural
concerns.

Construction Impacts and BCDC RSAP Guidelines

        The construction of appropriate nature-based shoreline infrastructure, to minimize impacts,
may require additional setbacks. The environmental impacts of construction and operation of a
ferry terminal, parking lot, and access road should be analyzed and either minimized or mitigated.
BCDC's RSAP guidelines will undoubtedly also influence how this shoreline infrastructure should
address sea level rise and utilize Natural and Nature Based solutions (NNBS) as part of the RSAP.
In addition, the proposed development site is on Bay fill and as sea levels rise, groundwater is also
expected to rise. These Bay fill soils are prone to liquefaction in the event of earthquakes which we
all know are inevitable in the Bay Area. This potential liquification should be addressed.

Issues Concerning Alternative Development Sites

       The EIR must analyze reasonable alternatives. An alternative that is not reasonable and that
should not be used is for a ferry terminal at the Albany Golden Gate Fields racetrack site. The
track is now closed. SPRAWLDEF has called for the entire Golden Gate Fields site to be acquired
and added to the MESP. SPRAWLDEF has also stated that after acquisition over time, the site
should be restored to its original wetland and marsh that covered most of the site in the early
1900's before it was filled for the track. This restoration would further BCDC's goals of restoring
and increasing wetlands and marsh in the Bay thus creating a resilient shoreline using NNBS which
is one of the primary goals of the BCDC RSAP.

Bay Fill and Groundwater Rise
The proposed ferry includes parking and other structures that are situated on bay fill, which is
prone to liquefaction in seismic events. Rising sea levels will also elevate groundwater levels, further
destabilizing these soils. This poses significant risks for the construction and long-term viability of
the site for a ferry terminal and need to be fully analyzed in the EIR.

Environmental Impact of Ferry Terminal
The construction and operation of the ferry terminal could detrimentally impact nearby sensitive
habitats especially the Conservation area on the Berkeley Meadow in the MESP, and the North and
South Basins. Increased boat wakes could harm migratory birds and other aquatic species. If the
ferries are not electric, then ferry diesel emissions pose a pollution risk. A Water Emergency Transit
                                                   2

SPRAWLDEF to Berkeley

Re: Berkeley Ferry NOP, 2025-05-19
Authority (WETA) study demonstrated that ferries create dead zones for waterfowl in the ferry
wake zone thus significantly impacting those species. Mitigations such as slow speed requirements
around recognized rafting duck locations should be considered as mitigation requirements.
Comprehensive mitigation strategies must be developed and evaluated to minimize these
environmental impacts. The potential impacts on bird species protected under the Migratory Bird
Treaty must be analyzed.

Potential for private ferries
We also continue to be extremely concerned about WETA's future plans to consider allowing
private ferries at various terminals. The project description includes the possible addition of special
event service. It does not specifically forbid private vehicles. If private ferries (that are both
scheduled and unscheduled) and water taxis (similar to calling an Uber or Lyft water taxi) are
allowed to use the dock and terminal facility, this presents a significant problem . It is important to
monitor and enforce speed restrictions of boats as well as to minimize the number of boats
through the refuge. It has been clearly demonstrated that it is difficult or impossible to do daily
enforcement of speed restrictions of private ferries or water taxis.
Additional boats, especially private ferries, and water taxis that are not obeying the speed
restrictions, would cause more environmental and safety concerns including more wake waves,
potential impacts on rowers and paddlers in non-motorized watercraft, shoreline erosion, and
impacts on birds and other aquatic species.

Air Quality
Evaluate the impact of ferry diesel emissions on recreational users of the waterway as well as
adjacent shoreline communities. If the project plan includes backup power using diesel fuel, include
those emissions in the analysis.

Artificial Light at Night (ALAN)

Due to proximity to MESP and protected waters, night lights from the terminal and parking areas
will be harmful to birds and other wildlife in the nearby MESP. ALAN interferes with bird
reproduction, feeding and migration. Night foraging creatures will not be able to forage if lights are
on at night and shine on the water. The EIR must evaluate approaches to and require minimizing
ALAN and lighting and use of the site after sundown.

Noise

       The EIR must evaluate the maximum decibel of the ferries and of other equipment at the
project site and their impact on birds and other wildlife. Ensure that there are no private boats
using the dock, especially at night, such as party boats or special event boats. Evaluate the impact
of construction period and noise including pile driving and length of construction time on
                                                   3

SPRAWLDEF to Berkeley

Re: Berkeley Ferry NOP, 2025-05-19
adjoining habitat and species. Considering the disruption and noise during the construction period,
will a significant area of this valuable wildlife habitat be no longer viable for wildlife that now
consider it home?

Bird Safe Design

       Bird-safe design principles are crucial for protecting avian populations, particularly in areas
adjacent to wildlife refuges. These principles aim to prevent bird collisions with structures, which is
a significant threat to bird safety. Structures such as buildings, windows, and other man-made
objects often pose hazards to birds, leading to injuries or fatalities. Implementing bird-safe designs
is essential to minimize these risks and promote a safe environment for birds, especially in areas
with high bird activity.

       The Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 (16 U.S.C. 703-712) provides that it is unlawful to
pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, possess, sell, purchase, barter, import, export, or transport any
migratory bird, or any part, nest, or egg or any such bird, unless authorized under a permit issued
by the Secretary of the Interior. Since the areas in the MESP and in and around the proposed
terminal site are used by migratory birds, the impact of the ferry on migratory birds must be
analyzed.

Geology, Soils, and Seismicity
The EIR must include information on the soils at the site as well as along the only access road that
gives access to the site. Soil settlement along the two mile access road indicates unstable soils.

Hazards and Hazardous Materials

Recent investigations have revealed that there are fill areas on the Albany, Berkeley, and Richmond
shorelines that have toxic and hazardous materials. A thorough review of historical and current
environmental data is necessary to assess potential contamination risks.

Utilities and Service Systems
The EIR must analyze the life service of existing utilities and storm water/wastewater systems.
Rising groundwater may be poised to inundate portions of the buried utilities off site that are
serving the site.

Transportation Issues from Increased Gas Powered Automobiles

       The ferry terminal will result in greater automobile use to and from the ferry terminal. The
increase in such especially from gas powered automobiles in terms of air quality and impacts from

cadmium and other toxic materials found in automobile tires must be analyzed, especially as to
impacts on wildlife and habitat in the MESP.

Re: Scoping Comments to Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Berkeley Water

Thank you for giving me the opportunity to add my comments to the following topics covered by
CEQA

Land Use Planning and Recreation

Inadequate Parking Studies and Latent Demand:
This is a very important area for study and is lacking from the current report, as pointed out by
various user groups and by the BCDC's DRC. The study's proposed landside improvements,
plus a new pier and a hospitality development at 199 Seawall, etc. in and by themselves will
attract more users. But it is also well known that these days the popularity of aquatic recreation
has soared (especially open water swimming), as have other activities like birdwatching, fishing,
kayaking or simply walking along the shoreline. Attention needs to be paid to quantify this.

It is challenging to assess future demand at the waterfront because so many of its popular
features have been closed for so long, including the fishing pier, Hs Lordships and more
recently the East Dock. The pedestrian trails are in such bad condition that it discourages their
use (this is especially relevant for seniors who like to walk along the water's edges for their
recreation, it is dangerous for them). All this must be factored in while assessing future parking
demand.

More studies and outreach efforts need to be made to target current user groups and mapping
their key areas of use (as per the BCDC's DRC).

Asserting that ferry riders would park along Marina Blvd demands further study. It is
inconceivable that ferry riders would walk 2400 to 3200 ft, and park their cars in an unpaved lot
that provides no safety oversight, even if parking there were free.

As has been pointed out by many others, there are too few data points in your study for prime
time usage by recreationists, this needs to be enhanced. And if a TDM program ascertains that
paid parking makes management that much easier, it does not account for the impacts it would
have on equity and public usage. It might make it "easier'' for a transit terminal but it would have
deleterious impact on attracting new users to the waterfront, something that both staff and policy
makers support.

Hazards and Hazardous Materials
Traffic and Transportation:
The intersection at University and Frontage Road is dangerous, especially during peak
commuter and recreation hours. A ferry with a set schedule will further exacerbate this, with
drivers "rushing" to park and then catch the ferry, and upon their return to rush home after work.
While adding traffic control devices would be Caltrans' responsibility, the NOP should recognize
the need for improvements and factor this in the analysis.
There have been no reports that reference impacts the ferry would have on other public transit
agencies, including BART and AC Transit that have much higher ridership numbers. Or how a
Berkeley terminal would affect Oakland's and Richmond's ferry service.

Hydrology and Water Quality
More attention needs to be paid to wave action and wake projections in this report.

Alternatives:
There has been no recognition in the EIR process that alternatives can exist beyond a rebuilt
pier. These include the docks that the Hornblower ties up, and the D&E docks as well.

Thank you for including my responses and observations.

First, I appreciated the way you ran this meeting, both soliciting input and speaking with candor. I hope that the
recording of the meeting, including slides, will be made available - but don't find it at the WSP website yet?

Now that I've had a chance to reflect, I'd like to share some thoughts/suggestions as well as additional concerns.

I believe you heard from many disparate users how important non-motorized launch access at His Lords Cove is and will
remain (including swimmers). That cove provides immediate access to deeper parts of the Bay as well as to the usual
seasonal Westerlies PM wind line. At the same time, I heard you express concern that "risks/legal constraints" might
preclude future development and use of that Cove. That, along with the phrase "under consideration" regarding Cove
improvements, definitely set off alarms.

The alternative access site you mentioned (just NE of His Lords on South Sailing Basin side - "Option 2"?), while perhaps
attractive from terrain and cost considerations, would basically negate the two most important attributes of the Cove
(see above). It is one thing to carry gear on ramps/ashore and quite another to swim it westward around the point to
access depth and wind, especially if you are trying to get upwind and fighting Mother Nature.

Another critical issue that everyone seemed sensitive to is the "final approach" to actually putting gear and bodies into
the water. At present, users must clamber down/up the riprap to access the relatively benign gravel/sand/muck path
below. High tide presents even more challenge as users struggle to see where to step under the surface prior to
reaching that path. I have decades of experience managing that process at the Cove - almost never pleasant. A solution
that doesn't address that will be a major concern.

Some suggestions:

1. I don't know who you are consulting with regarding actual launch improvement design? For the Pt. Isabel project I
worked with Kyle MacDonald, the coastal engineer initially via CLE Engineering, which subsequently became Foth/CLE
Engineering. I'd suggest early and close involvement of users with actual planners/engineers would be much more likely
to produce good outcomes. That was precisely my experience with EBRPD and Foth for the Pt. Isabel project. Prior to
final design and construction, I gave rigging/launch demonstrations to involved staff to clarify constraints and access
needs, etc.

2. At Pt. Isabel, the "breakthrough" came when we decided on two ramps - an ADA version (5% max grade) and a more
immediate/practical steeper version (20%). However, as you will see in photo right below showing my gear and the
"meeting pad" of the two ramps, that approach still begs the question of the "final approach" given terrain at His Lords.

3. I also remain concerned about access improvements at the Cove given the uncertainty of the HLS restaurant's
future. For example, if it were to be demolished, I expect we'd have much more design freedom.

Point Isabel Water Access and Safety Improvement Project

Existing Launch Access/Safety:
Replace the existing cement steps with a more accessible and stable textured ramp.
Add comparable-sized gravel to launch pathway above and below water line.

Remove submerged rock launch hazards to a minimum of 4 feet clearance below water surface at low tide in front of the

Rigging Area

rigging area.
Additional Site and Safety Improvements
Add an appropriately surfaced pathway from road to rigging area to launch site.
Add wash-down capability at rigging area (water accessed from existing supply to Park toilets or Radio Bldg).
Remove boulders currently blocking base of Dog Ramp (emergency egress site).

RE:           Public Input on NOP of Draft EIR for Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry

Dear Ms. McNulty

Thank you for taking my input on the NOP for the EIR of the Pier-Ferry Project and Waterfront
Specific Plan. I am a Berkeley resident writing as a private citizen, in my own capacity. I have
followed the planning effort at the Berkeley Waterfront closely since January 2018, when the
findings for replacing the Berkeley Pier were shared with the public at the regular monthly
meeting of the Parks and Waterfront Commission.

This submission addresses the following topics:

          OVERVIEW
          ALTERNATIVES
          BASELINE
          PARKING DATA & LATENT DEMAND
          BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES during a GLOBAL BIODIVERSITY CRISIS
          SITE VISITS for BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES
          STUDY BOUNDARY AND DATA for BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES
          ROAD MORTALITIES: COLLISIONS KILL BIRDS, MONARCHS, and COUNTLESS OTHER SPECIES
          LIGHT POLLUTION
          NOISE POLLUTION
          SHIP STRIKES
          ENERGY EFFICIENCY and GREEN HOUSE GASES
          SHORELINE DISTURBANCE and TURBIDITY


OVERVIEW

At the highest level, and from the very beginning, I remain concerned about the bifurcation of
the planning efforts of the Pier/Ferry and the Waterfront Specific Plan (WSP). This artificial split
has hindered the accurate assessment of the cumulative impacts of the ferry and potential
development in other areas of the Waterfront/Marina area - including recreational access, the
environment, local & migratory species, equity, public health, and more.


[Type here]                                Berkeley Ferry EIR NOP (EDiehm)                      1 of 21
The bifurcation of the Pier-ferry project from the WSP is a kind of piecemealing which is not
allowed under CEQA law. For example, and more recently, in their presentation to the Parks,
Recreation and Waterfront Commission at their regular meeting in May 2025, Berkeley Staff
described how overflow parking for the ferry would now be designated for the Skates parking
lot and along Marina Boulevard. These locations had been illustrated in earlier versions of the
WSP as the potential location of a new hotel &/or parking. Thus, the ferry and WSP are
bleeding into each other and are truly one single project, and should be evaluated as such.

ALTERNATIVES

To adhere to CEQA law, the EIR should address potentially feasible alternatives, that may be
environmentally &/or economically superior, including, but not limited to:
    1. a pier-only/no-ferry option - at the location of the currently closed pier. Until its
       closure, the pier (and associated fishing) offered important recreational opportunities
       and food security for many (valued in the millions of dollars, as documented by C.
       Antinori Ph.D., et al 1) Separately, on January 10, 2018 the results of a cost analysis for
       replacing just the pier (no ferry) were shared with the public at the Parks & Waterfront
       Commission. 2 Numerous scenarios were cost-estimated. Four of them ("Replacements"
       P8, P9, Pl0 and Pll) ranged in cost from $21-24M with an encouraging longevity of "55
       to 70" years. In spite of the hopefulness of these findings, discussion of a pier-only
       replacement did not continue and all further discussions of the pier involved the
       addition of a high-speed ferry. Moreover, many in the community have expressed their
       support for a pier-only option; it should be included as an Alternative in the EIR.
    2. locating the ferry terminal inside the Marina, on the North side of the interior of the
       Marina near the current-day DoubleTree, with a potentially smaller ferry. This location
       offers several benefits: (a) environmentally, by eliminating the need for new harmful
       dredging on the western edge where the currently closed pier is located (outside the
       Marina), thereby minimizing the dredging for the project, (b) maintaining recreational
       access, by having ferry users park in the dry-dock parking lot (on the north side), the lots
       on the south side of the Marina will remain open and the land designed for recreational
       use on the south side will remain available to those users (recreational access won't
       have been usurped by the ferry).

BASELINE

To ensure that the Baseline reflects the true current demand, and not an artificially low one, the
Baseline of recreational usage should incorporate recent prior usage, prior to the closure of 4


1 A newer version of this article may be available from the authors. This is the version referenced above: "Fishing at

the Berkeley Waterfront: What is it Worth?" by Camille Antinori Ph.D. et al. San Francisco State University, Sept 12,
2022., https://drive.google.com/file/d/14Gipko8qHsZxlFd4c6BHdiZzB8Pw-Alt/view
2 Berkeley Municipal Pier Renovation Alternatives.

https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/COB%20-%20Alternative%20Summary%20Table edits.pdf



[Type here]                                  Berkeley Ferry EIR NOP (EDiehm)                                     2 of 21
facilities that attracted many people to the Waterfront, namely: the fishing pier, Hs Lordships
and its parking lot, the East dock, and the lot currently fenced off for use by parking
enforcement. The Baseline should not be based on usage in 2025 at the time of the NOP, when
these 4 facilities are closed and inaccessible to the public, which drives down activity and would
give an artificially low, inaccurate assessment of true need and current usage.

FOR EIR SCOPE: To ensure accurate and proper assessment of usage, the Baseline should be
based on activity that includes (1) a reopened 2,000-ft pier, plus (2) the reopened Hs Lordships
space & lot, plus (3) the reopened East dock, plus (4) the reopened lot currently fenced off for
parking enforcement.


PARKING DATA & LATENT DEMAND

The current version of Kittelson's parking study for the pier-ferry project requires additional
work, because the scope of the data is insufficient. It doesn't include data for summer months
(times of peak use) and it combines data across all locations, ignoring specific uses in specific
locations and users' specific needs (like bringing equipment). The data also do not account for
latent demand-specifically, the increase in visitorship that is reasonably expected following the
restoration of the pier and the addition of new amenities in the marina area.

FOR EIR SCOPE: Under CEQA, environmental review must consider foreseeable changes
resulting from a project, and increased activity and visitation due to enhanced public attractions
are both foreseeable and significant. Therefore, I request that the parking analysis be revised to
include data for each individual lot, at times of day/year in the summer that reflect true peak
usage, include when parking visitors bring with them equipment to use with the recreational
activity, and projections for latent demand, ensuring that the Environmental Impact Report fully
reflects the project's likely impacts on parking availability and transportation infrastructure.


BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES during a GLOBAL BIODIVERSITY CRISIS

It is widely recognized that we are in a global biodiversity crisis. Scientists predict that on our
current trajectory, nearly 40% of all species will face extinction by 21003 . Insects are in steep
decline (e.g. up to a 75% loss if insect biomass since 1990, the "Insect Apocalypse" 4 ; a 22%
decline in butterfly species from 2000-2022, plus an ongoing additional 2% loss per year 5 ). Birds
are in trouble, too. Since the 1970s almost one-third of all birds have disappeared from the U.S. 6

back

FOR EIR SCOPE: El Rs typically limit evaluation of Biological Resources to an extremely short list
of formally listed species, which results in very few species being considered and the vast
majority of others being ignored, potentially putting many in harm's way. Given the biological
importance of the proposed project site (locally and regionally), coupled with the alarming

7 "State of the Birds 2025"      https://www.stateofthebirds.org/2025/executive-summary/
8 ibid.

global declines in biodiversity, it is appropriate and I request that the EIR cast a wider net when
evaluating which species to consider as a "Biological Resource", to include species that aren't
listed (and are being considered for listing), and to evaluate comprehensive impacts of the
proposed high-speed ferry system, including increased vehicle traffic to the Marina (and
associated collisions with insects, birds, and wildlife), light pollution, noise (above and below
water), and more.


SITE VISITS for BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES

Migratory species may be present in some months and absent in others. If site visits occur when
a migratory species aren't present, the impact on those species will be ignored.

FOR EIR SCOPE: To ensure a comprehensive evaluation of Biological Resources under CEQA, I
request that a number of site visits be conducted, across multiple seasons and key biological
windows. This approach is critical to accurately document the presence or absence of migratory
species, breeding activity, and other seasonally dependent ecological factors. Site assessments
limited to a narrow timeframe risk overlooking important biological indicators and could result
in an incomplete or inaccurate impact analysis.


STUDY BOUNDARY AND DATA for BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES

The boundary of study as presented in the NOP is too small to accurately assess real impacts on
Biological Resources by the proposed Berkeley ferry and the larger WETA ferry system. The
boundary described in the NOP is limited to University Avenue, the proposed ferry Plaza, 3
nearby parking lots, the Pier and waters nearby north and south; illustrated below (from the
NOP):




               ~   PotentialCons1ruction
                   Staging Areas




[Type here]                                Berkeley Ferry EIR NOP (EDiehm)                     5 of 21
                                              Area of Study as proposed in the NOP, April 18, 2025.


Birds and other species, readily move throughout the larger marina area, to forage, find nesting
material, hunt, and more. It is unreasonable to limit the boundary to such a small area and think
it will assess the real impacts on nearby species. A bird that lives in Sylvia Mclaughlin Eastshore
State Park, or in the Marina, may forage in the vegetation at Shorebird Park or in the water
along the shoreline affected by the high-speed ferry. The boundary should, therefore, be
expanded.

Ensuring adequate assessment is especially important because Berkeley's Waterfront/Marina is
of high global ecological significance. It lies within the San Francisco Bay, the largest estuary on
the West Coast and one of North America's most important ... recognized as an international
biodiversity hotspot ... [and a] key stopover along on the Pacific" 9 with millions of birds
migrating through at peak season .

To evaluate the biological resources at the Waterfront, the EIR should use the globally-utilized
and -recognized citizen-science platforms iNaturalist and eBird 10 to ensure that all species
inhabiting the Marina/Waterfront area -year-round residents & migratory, listed & not-listed -
are documented and adequately protected from unnecessary harm .

iNaturalist data shows that 1,178 total species have been documented in the larger Berkeley
Marina area, illustrated below 11 (this includes 196 species of birds, not illustrated, but Filters
can focus on avian species):

The nesting & feeding patterns of birds and other creatures cover a broad area. For example, a
bird that nests on the east side of the Marina, may hunt in Shorebird park. A snake that lives in
the Sylvia Mclaughlin Eastshore State Park may crawl south across University Avenue to forage,
but be killed by an oncoming vehicle while crossing the road.

FOR EIR SCOPE: To ensure a complete and adequate assessment, the EIR should not base its
analysis of Biological Resources on on-site visits alone. Those visits are inherently limited in time
and scope, making them insufficient to evaluate the presence of migratory species throughout



[Type here]                                               Berkeley Ferry EIR NOP (EDiehm)                                                                     12 of 21
the year. To ensure a full and complete analysis of Biological Resources, reliable and more
comprehensive data sources available online should be utilized, too. I request that the EIR
incorporate relevant data from iNaturalist and eBird in its evaluation Biological Resources.

I also request that the study boundary for biological resources in the EIR be expanded to
encompass the full range of habitat areas functionally connected to the project site, as many
species rely on spatially distinct but ecologically linked areas for critical life functions such as
foraging, nesting, and migration, and a narrowly defined boundary may fail to capture
significant impacts on their survival. I request that the expanded boundary cover the larger
Waterfront area, including:

     •    University Avenue, extending south to the South Basin shoreline
     •    Sylvia McLaughlin Eastshore State Park
     •    North Basin
     •    Cesar Chavez Park
     •    Berkeley Marina (landside and basin)
     •    Shorebird Park & Seawall Area (formerly Hs Lordships and lot)
     •    the Plaza, pier, and nearby waters

assessed, I request that leading local conservation organizations are contacted for their input on
the EIR, especially:
    • The Golden Gate Bird Alliance (https://goldengatebirdalliance.org)
    • Marine Mammal Center (https://www.marinemammalcenter.org)

LIGHT POLLUTION

Artificial Light At Night (ALAN) is a major environmental disruptor.

ALAN can interfere with organisms at all levels - from those in the soil, to insects, aquatic
species 20, birds, and even humans (where it is associated with certain kinds of cancers). ALAN is
a major driver of global insect declines 21 . Light pollution negatively impacts birds, too,
disrupting nesting behavior and even bird global migrations 22 -birds are lured off course, into
urban areas, where they face numerous threats. Birds making the flight for the first time are
especially vulnerable.

With the advent of energy-efficient LEDs, the cost of lighting has greatly decreased causing the
use of LEDs to proliferate. Global light pollution is now increasing at 2% per year. 23 DarkSky
International offers guidelines for outdoor lighting 24 outlining "5 Principles for Responsible
Outdoor Lighting" 25

FOR EIR SCOPE: The EIR should include a robust evaluation of all potential new light pollution
associated with the proposed ferry project and mitigations. It should include potentially
introduced light, as part of the proposed pier-ferry at just Berkeley, as well as across the entire
ferry system, including the existing 10 Terminals and the proposed 27 total future Terminals, to
determine the true cumulative impacts of the WETA ferry system on our Bay environment.


NOISE POLLUTION

Whether all-electric or diesel, the WETA high-speed ferries contribute to the growing
anthropogenic cacophony in the Bay waters. The article "The soundscape of the Anthropocene
ocean" 26 offers many helpful statements about the noise risks of the proposed high speed ferry
system on marine life in the Bay, including this Outlook,

           "Anthropogenic noise is a stressor for marine animals. Thus, we call for it to be included
           in assessments of cumulative pressures on marine ecosystems. Compared with other
           stressors that are persistent in the environment, such as carbon dioxide emitted to the
           atmosphere or persistent organic pollutants delivered to marine ecosystems,
           anthropogenic noise is typically a point-source pollutant, the effects of which decline
           swiftly once sources are removed. The evidence summarized here encourages national
           and international policies to become more ambitious in regulating and deploying
           existing technological solutions to mitigate marine noise and improve the human
           stewardship of ocean soundscapes to maintain a healthy ocean." 27

and regarding noise as pollution,

           This "anthropogenic noise", (introduced by ferries and other sources), "is a pollutant
           that cannot be ignored ... it must be mitigated to reduce human impacts" 28 on the ocean

Now let's look at WETA's current and proposed ferry system, in light of the anthropogenic noise
that will be introduced to the Bay waters. At writing there are 10 Terminals but WETA's Business
Plan identifies 26 total Terminals system-wide, stretching the length of the Bay, from Pittsburg-
Antioch (in the north, on the Delta), all the way down south to Sunnyvale-San Jose-Milpitas (at
the very southern reach of the Bay).

With each new terminal, the noise pollution introduced into the Bay environment by the WETA
ferry system will increase. Given the frequency of routes and the reach of this system, the noise
disruptions could be significant, extensive and virtually Bay-wide, possibly introducing
"harassment" of aquatic species.

FOR EIR SCOPE: Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which requires
analysis of all potentially significant environmental impacts of a proposed project, I request that
the Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the proposed high-speed ferry terminal in Berkeley
include a thorough assessment of noise pollution-both above and below water-generated by
ferry operations - for both electric and diesel vessels. This analysis should address the specific
impacts at the proposed Berkeley terminal, as well as the cumulative impacts associated with
the current system of 10 terminals, as well as the full build-out of 26 terminals, as required
under CEQA Guidelines §15130 regarding cumulative impacts. Given the well-documented
sensitivity of aquatic and shoreline wildlife to noise pollution, particularly from high-speed
vessels, the EIR must evaluate potential effects on local and migratory species, including those
protected under state and federal law. This analysis is essential to ensure compliance with
CEQA's mandate to avoid or mitigate significant environmental impacts wherever feasible.


SHIP STRIKES

Ship strikes are a known disruptor and cause of death for aquatic species. For example, 5 gray
whales have recently stranded and died in the Bay Area. One was confirmed due to a ship
strike 35 . High-speed vessels, particularly quiet electric ferries, pose an increased risk to whales
and other aquatic species due to reduced detectability. The WETA ferry system currently has 10
Terminals and plans to expand to 26 total. Every additional Terminal, with multiple routes per
day multiplies the threat to marine mammals and other wildlife.

FOR EIR SCOPE: I request that the EIR specifically evaluate the risk of ship strikes and other
disruptions due to turbulence on all aquatic species, across the entire ferry system, specifically,
for ferries at (a) just the Berkeley site, (b) ferries cumulatively across the existing 10 Terminals,
and (c) ferries cumulatively across the proposed expanded 26 Terminals.

The Marine Mammal Center (https://www.marinemammalcenter.org) conducts important
research on ship strikes. I request that the EIR team reach out to them for input and guidance
on this important topic.


ENERGY EFFICIENCY and GREEN HOUSE GASES

At community meetings early-on in the planning of the proposed pier-ferry, we in the
community (myself included) asked several times for information about energy efficiency of the

35 "Fifth dead whale found in San Francisco Bay" by Ryan Mense at KRON4, April 21, 2025.

https://www.kron4.com/news/bay-area/fifth-dead-whale-found-in-san-francisco-bay/



[Type here]                                Berkeley Ferry EIR NOP (EDiehm)                       20 of 21
ferries. To date we have not received an answer. We want to know how much energy the ferries
- diesel and electric - use per passenger mile (expressed as BTUs per passenger mile). We want
to compare that efficiency with other forms of transit for crossing the Bay (e.g. BART, or a fully
loaded bus) to determine if the ferry is the environmentally superior alternative.

Second, while the ferry has been described as an all-electric "zero emission", the generation of
the energy to supply the batteries will likely involve burning of fossil fuels off site, generating
GHGs. In addition, many ferry riders will drive a gasoline-powered car to the Marina to take the
ferry (instead of walking or biking to their local bus or BART stop), emitting GHGs.

FOR EIR SCOPE: Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines§ 15126.2(b) and Appendix F, I request that the
Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the proposed high-speed ferry terminal include a
comprehensive analysis of energy use and energy efficiency associated with both the
construction and operation of the project. This should include, but not be limited to, fuel
consumption for ferry vessels, electricity and energy demands of terminal facilities, and any
supporting infrastructure. I request that the energy use (for the ferries, expressed as BTUs per
passenger mile) be compared with other forms of transit across the Bay (e.g. BART). The
analysis should evaluate whether the project would result in wasteful, inefficient, or
unnecessary consumption of energy.
I also request that a comprehensive evaluation of GHGs emitted, off-site for powering the
ferries & their operations, as well as locally from the fuel for passenger vehicles.


SHORELINE DISTURBANCE and TURBIDITY

I remain extremely concerned that the proposed high-speed ferry system will significantly
increase disturbance and turbidity along our Bay shoreline, degrading the biological stability of
the shoreline and negatively impacting biological resources, including benthic organisms, birds
that hunt along the shallow shoreline and the fish that anglers depend on.

FOR EIR SCOPE: I request that the EIR for the proposed high-speed ferry terminal include a
detailed analysis of the potential for increased shoreline disturbance and turbidity resulting
from ferry operations. This analysis should address localized impacts near the proposed
terminal in Berkeley, including wake-induced erosion, sediment resuspension from vessel prop
wash, and degradation of nearshore habitats. In addition, consistent with CEQA Guidelines§
15130, the EIR should evaluate the cumulative impacts of the existing and proposed ferry
system-currently 10 terminals and potentially up to 26 in the future-on shoreline integrity
and water quality throughout the Bay. Repeated vessel activity can contribute to long-term
habitat degradation, reduced water clarity, and the loss of biologically important intertidal
zones, particularly in shallow or enclosed areas.



Best regards,
Erin Diehm

     An anthropogenic cacophony
             Sound travels faster and farther in water than in air. Over evolutionary time, many marine organisms have come




                                                                                                                              Downloaded from http://science.sciencemag.org/ on February 11, 2021
     to rely on sound production, transmission, and reception for key aspects of their lives. These important behaviors are
     threatened by an increasing cacophony in the marine environment as human-produced sounds have become louder and
     more prevalent. Duarte et al. review the importance of biologically produced sounds and the ways in which
     anthropogenically produced sounds are affecting the marine soundscape.

Liza,

This email, sent in March 2022, called attention to issues arising from the very exposed location of the proposed WETA
ferry dock. Most importantly, a loss of control event at a critical point of the ferry's approach to the dock could cause
the ferry to run onto the rocks or collide with the Skate's restaurant, with considerable risk of injury or damage. The
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry EIR must address this possibility.

       •   What is the probability of a loss of control (LOC) event in the ferries serving Berkeley?
       •   What would be the protocol for dealing with an LOC event in a ferry approaching the Berkeley WETA dock? E.g.,
           rapid deployment of an anchor?
       •   What initial and ongoing training is necessary to ensure that the appropriate protocol is successfully followed
           whenever an LOC occurs?
       •   Alternatively, the ferry dock could be relocated inside the Marina or another sheltered location.

Assuming this major safety issue can be addressed, consider next the storms that would be expected every year,

       •   How often would storms with strong North or South winds require ferry service to be suspended?
       •   How would the service suspension be communicated to ferry patrons?
       •   What alternate transportation would be available and how would ferry patrons access it?
       •   Again, it would probably be best to locate the ferry dock in a sheltered area and avoid these service suspensions

                                                                 2
  Wind, Waves, and Lee Shore at the WETA Ferry Dock Location




This is a still picture from a video (attached, I suggest you watch it) of conditions in Berkeley's
south sailing basin with a strong south wind blowing directly across the south-facing
seawall. Note the reflected waves, and the spray overtopping the seawall. With a strong
north wind, the proposed north-facing WETA dock would probably look something like the
video, with waves breaking over the dock and soaking anyone on it.

North and South Winds
Strong North and South wind events happen several times a year on the Bay. The figure below
shows the Sword configuration presented at Workshop #2. Wave protection looks good for the
predominant west-to-southwest wind directions, but strong North to Northwest wind and waves
would hit the WETA docks with full force, with waves overtopping the docks much like the
waves in the video. Protecting the WETA docks against waves coming from the north is not at
all easy because a breakwater cannot be placed within or directly upwind of the ferry turning
basin. This is a serious problem for a dock in this location, which probably would mean
cancelling ferry service on days with north winds above a certain threshold.

For a South wind, the 'Sword' hilt forms (as labeled in the figure) a Protected Berthing Position,
but if there is no wave attenuation for the Lower Wave Condition berth, waves would probably
overtop the float in full view of passengers waiting in line for the ferry in the Protected Berthing
Position. Entertaining, perhaps, but not confidence-inspiring. Wave attenuation for south wind
storms needs to be present for both the Lower Wave Condition berth and the Protected Berthing
Position.




                                                  1
Nearby Lee Shore
In the usual westerly summer winds, an inbound ferry will come downwind to a position north of
the ferry's berth, then make a 180° turn in the "Ferry Turning Basin" so it ends up pointed
upwind when docked. But the summer winds are often well above 25 mph, and the waves can be
substantial, a bit like those in the picture above. The 180° turn would at the very least give the
ferry captains a good chance to demonstrate their skill.
There is a significant hazard here, however: the ferry turning basin is just a few boat lengths
upwind of both the rocky shore and the Skates restaurant. If a ferry were to lose power or
steering control just before the 180° turn, it would not take long for the ferry's eastward motion,
helped by a strong summer wind, to carry it down to the shore. It might ground on the rocks,
which would be dangerous, or collide with the Skates restaurant, which would be very dangerous
indeed. Skates is built on tall, slender pilings (see below) and might not survive a collision with
a 135-foot-long ferry, especially if the ferry were to drift under the restaurant. The chance of
injury in such an accident would be significant.

Perhaps after a power loss there would be time and room to set an anchor, perhaps not-an
anchor would have to be dropped almost immediately after loss of power to have a chance of
stopping the ferry in time. For the crew to deal with such a situation, they must have appropriate
equipment and rigorous training in how to use it, very much like the training aircraft pilots
receive for engine failures during takeoffs.




                                                 2
With well-maintained ferries, this kind of power loss should be a very rare event. Given the
potential hazard involved, though, I think this is a safety issue that needs to be carefully
evaluated for this site.

WETA's new Treasure Island ferry dock also has a windy location and a close lee shore-and,
for what it's worth, a breakwater to protect against north winds and waves. Perhaps WETA has
investigated this problem. If so, they should share their work.




Wind and Wave Modeling
In 2018, the city commissioned a study by GHD, Small Scale Ferry Terminal FS Berkeley
Municipal Pier_DRAFTpdf, that should have helped with the design of the pier and the
identification of the lee shore problem. Unfortunately, the study used wind data from NOAA's
Alameda Station, a far less windy location than the Berkeley Marina, so the wave modeling was
for 12 mph west wind and was therefore useless (see pages iii, 24, and 25). If the Berkeley Pier
docking site is to be used, a wind and wave study should be completed using real-world data,
probably obtainable from iWindsurf, which has several nearby wind sensors and archives of
wind strength/direction data. This data should allow modeling wave action for all wind
directions, and so guide the design of wave protection for the ferry docks. Modeling should
include prediction of silting resulting from candidate breakwater designs.




                                                3
Pier Structure Design
The design of the pier structure also needs consideration: the design chosen has monopile bents
along the pier centerline, unlike the existing pier which has its pilings along the north and south
pier edges.

This design choice has safety implications: the centerline structure makes it much more likely
that a boat that gets blown against the pier will end up under the pier deck (see picture below of a
boat blown under the San Mateo bridge in 2009). Widening the stance of the two concrete pile
bents and keeping the along-pier pile spacing low would provide better protection against a boat
ending up under the pier.
(Figures above from study by GHD, Small Scale Ferry Terminal FS Berkeley Municipal
Pier_DRAFTpdf, pages 11 and 12.)




                                                 4
                                                                                         Michael Macor / The Chronicle

Picture/story:
https://www .sfgate.com/bayarea/article/Crews-to-move-boat-stuck-at-San-Mateo-Bridge-3 I 65070.php#photo-2297 687

In addition to the safety implications, the location of the piles has implications for fishing from
the pier, since the pilings and the biomass that attaches to them are part of the food chain of fish
and crabs. The current pier construction allows fishing directly adjacent to the pier support
pilings, which, if I remember from long ago, gets more bites. This should be looked into before
finalizing the design. Keeping part of the underwater structure of the old pier should also be
considered.

Dredge the North Marina Entrance
As a person who goes in and out of the marina under sail, I would choose to use the north harbor
entrance at times when both ferries and fishing charter boats are likely to be using the south
entrance. Therefore, I think that the ferry project should undertake the dredging of the north
harbor entrance as well as the south one, so that boats leaving and entering the marina have the
opportunity to avoid possible congestion near the ferry dock.

                    WETA's Berkeley Ferry Dock Location




On November 23, 2018 a Golden Gate Ferry rammed a dock at the San Francisco Ferry building,
check out the bow damage in the picture above and this video. Fortunately, there were no serious
injuries and damage was relatively minor, about $3 million. The cause of the accident appears to
have been the captain's unfamiliarity with a recently upgraded control system

                                               1
Consider the possibility of a similar loss of control accident happening at the dock location
proposed for the Berkeley WETA ferry (see below). In the usual westerly summer winds
("Wind Direction" arrow in the figure), an inbound ferry will come in along the "Ferry
Approach" arrow, then make a 180° turn in the "Ferry Turning Basin" so it ends up pointed
upwind when it gets to the dock. But the summer afternoon winds are often well above 25 mph,
and the waves are substantial. The 180° turn would at the very least give the ferry captains a
good chance to demonstrate their skill.




FINAL_Ferry Terminal Facility Feasibility Study - Berkeley Municipal Pier   See Page 34 (arrows added)



Zoomed-in image showing Dorado-sized (~300 passenger) ferry halfway through a 180° turn.




                                                    2
It is a very tight situation for a possible control loss. The inshore end of the ferry's dock is only
200 feet upwind of the rocky shore, and a 25-mph wind would soon push a disabled ferry
downwind onto the rocks, which would be quite dangerous, or onto the Skates restaurant, which
would be very dangerous indeed. Skates is built on tall, slender pilings (see next page) and
might not survive wind and wave pushing a 135-foot-long ferry against and perhaps underneath
it. Injuries and damage in such an accident would be very likely.

Information with some bearing on how likely a control loss event might be:
    1. The meeting minutes of the Harbor Safety Committee of the San Francisco Bay Region
       for January and February 2025 described seven instances of loss of propulsion or steering
       in passenger vessels on the Bay. (see Harbor Safety Committee Reports of Loss of
       Propulsion Jan and Feb 2025.pdf, attached with this document).
    2. Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis are recalling over 146,000 electric vehicles because a faulty
       part may cause them to lose power while driving. In addition to the main traction
       batteries, a typical EV needs another power source (e.g. a 12V battery) to run the
       controls. On an electric ferry, it is likely also a small battery, either backed up with a
       generator or not.
    3. After the Baltimore bridge collapse caused by a power loss in a big container ship, USA
       Today summarized US Coast Guard data showing: At least 6,000 times in the past 22
       years - an average of more than five times a week - crews on board massive cargo ships,
       oil tankers, container barges and even cruise vessels have reported what befell the Dali: a
       loss of power, loss of propulsion, loss of steering, or some combination of the three ...

Docking Maneuvers:
   • The ferry battery will be at a low state of charge when the ferry arrives at Berkeley,
      which may exacerbate some system failure modes.
   • To the extent that the docking maneuvers involve dramatic steering or propulsion inputs,
      they may stress the control system and cause an incipient control failure to manifest as a
      hard failure during the docking.
   • The 180° turn requires the skipper to shift attention from starboard to port, which can be
      tricky given that the ferry's beam is 34.5 feet.
   • If the approach requires the ferry to drop backwards into position, the helmsman must
      look backwards to the dock, again, maybe tricky.
   • the loss of control occurs before the ferry slows for the 180° turn, the ferry's downwind
      If
      speed will greatly reduce the available time to respond.
   • ferry going downwind at 20 knots would take just over a minute to travel 200 feet to
      A
      the rocks. That does not leave much time to recognize and respond to a problem.

The best response to a loss of control event would probably be to drop an anchor. But an anchor
would need to be dropped very quickly, given the short drift distance available.

    o   What kind of anchor should be used, and how much scope will the anchor need?
    o   Will the anchor be dropped off the stem or bow? There probably need to be two
        protocols, one for an anchor drop before the 180° turn and another for an anchor drop
        after the turn.


                                                  3
    o Will the mud bottom be free of snags and debris that might keep the anchor from biting
      into the mud?
    o Is there anything on the underside of the ferry that the anchor line could foul?
    o Are there enough crew on the ferries to deploy the anchor quickly?
    o When the anchor line comes tight, is there potential for injury to people near it?

The approach of the ferry to the dock and the dropping of the anchor would need carefully
thought-out protocols, which ferry personnel would need to be well-trained to execute rapidly if
a loss of control event occurs.

In my opinion, the WETA dock should be positioned in a less exposed site, for example inside
the Marina or in a purpose-designed facility on the Golden Gate Fields shoreline.

This is a matter that should be carefully considered in the ferry project EIR.

Harbor Safety Committee of the San Francisco Bay Region
February 13, 2025
https://www.sfmx.org/wp-content/uploads/2025-02 HSCMinutes DRAFT.pdf
Total of 29 entries, the four below were LOP for passenger vessels
Loss of Propulsion (17DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced a Loss of Propulsion
on the port engine. Vessel moored safely at San Francisco Gate B and received permission for a
one-time transit from San Francisco to Larkspur for repairs. Coast Guard issued the vessel an
Operational Control, rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). On 07JAN2025, vessel
operator reported the root cause of the loss of propulsion as a failed fuel injector. On
21JAN2025, Coast Guard received a report that the vessel propulsion system operated as
intended following satisfactory sea trials. Deficiency Cleared. Case pends.

Loss of Propulsion (23DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced a reduction in
propulsion on the starboard engine due to a low fuel oil pressure alarm. Vessel received
permission from the Coast Guard for one time transit to Alameda facility to identify root cause,
provide tech report, and conduct sea trials. Coast Guard issued an Operational Control, rectify
Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). On 01JAN2025, Coast Guard received an email
outlining the root cause of the reduction in propulsion to be from an issue with the ECU
connecting to the starboard main engine. Vessel replaced the ECU and completed
satisfactory sea trials. Operational Control Cleared. Case Pends.

Loss of Propulsion {27DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced an engine stall while
transiting in the San Francisco Bay. Vessel returned to Pier 3 in Alameda and determined the
engine stall occurred due to a leaky fuel fitting. Vessel crew also found a loose connection at a
fuel hardline which caused air intrusion into the fuel system. Coast Guard issued an operational
control, rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). Crew repaired the faulty connection
and engine reached full RPM during satisfactory sea trials. Operational Control Cleared. Case
Pends.

Operational Control (23DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel received an operational control,
rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). Vessel reported loss of throttle control to port
and starboard propulsion drives while mooring at Pier 41. On 26DEC2024, operator submitted a
tech report that no abnormalities were found, sea trials conducted satisfactorily, and all systems
operational. Operational Control Cleared. On 27DEC2024, during transit, the vessel experienced
loss of throttle control to the port and starboard propulsion drives. Vessel moored at Pier 41.
Coast Guard issued an operational control, rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701).
Vessel received authorization for one-time transit to Pier 9 for maintenance and repairs. On
10JAN2025, the vessel conducted sea trials. While underway the operator completed several
propulsion tests, including full ahead followed by full astern. On 14JAN2025, technicians
reported that the throttles were calibrated to disable themselves until RPMs reduced below 70
when going from ahead to astern. Vessel installed new throttle controls. Operational control
Cleared. Case Closed.

Parking-TOM Response for PRWC meeting May 14, 2025 G. Stout
The parking studies that have been reported do not provide a comprehensive and accurate picture of
recreational parking at the marina. Without such a picture, neither good parking plans nor a credible
EIR is possible.

        Much of the parking data was compromised by the fact that years' worth of the parking records
       were collected at 10 am and 8 pm, and hence did not accurately reflect recreational use.

        Waterfront Monitors Parking Counts Page 22/129: "The City of Berkeley Waterfront Monitors
       have been consistently collecting daily parking counts at the Waterfront since May 2021. The
       data is collected by counting the number of occupied spaces at each lot at 10 am and 8 pm, with
       the results recorded on a paper survey form that is later entered into a spreadsheet maintained
       by Waterfront staff."

       "Limitations: The data may not reflect peak utilization which could occur outside of the hours of
       10 am and 8 pm. In Spring, 2024, staff began collecting data at additional time points (2 pm and
       4 pm), which was not used for this study due to the comparatively limited number of data
       points"

        Kittelson's 10 am-8pm data Limitations caveat highlights a problem that still shows up in the
        report. For example, Figure 5: Parking Utilization on Weekends (Average Saturday vs Peak
       Saturday), presumably this figure summarizes 10 am/8 pm data, but what time is midday, 2 or 4,
       or something else? And does the peak Saturday "overall public parking 75% occupied with 306
       spaces remaining" refer to empty spaces in slip holder lots? This is waterfront staff data, was in
       collected at 10 am? And what is the "Seawall Drive/Shorebird Lot"?

       It is probably true that Kittleson was set up to fail by a decision to keep the 10 am/8 pm data,
        but fail they did, it's confusing to read.

       On the plus side, Kittelson did present the Quality Counts data, collected on

                   ■   Saturday, April 6, 2024
                   ■   Thursday, April 11, 2024
                   ■   Thursday, August 1, 2024
                   ■   Thursday, August 22, 2024
                   ■   Saturday, August 24, 2024

       Five days of data for a multi-million-dollar project seems woefully inadequate, however.
        presented to the PRWC a study of sixteen Google Earth images of the Skates parking lot,
        because the Waterfront Specific Plan wanted to place a hotel there. Of the 16 images, a third
       showed a significant number of cars, a third showed few cars, and a third fell in between.

                                                  1                               05-April-2025 G. Stout
       Parking at the marina is variable, data sampling must be frequent enough to provide an
       accurate picture.

       But even if it is not enough data for designing a parking plan, maybe we can learn something
       from these five days of Quality Counts data. Tables 1 and 2 show that on weekends the South
       Cove East and West lots are both extremely full, way fuller than the earlier waterfront monitor
       data showed. And way too full--adding even a few spillover ferry rider's cars would make South
       Cove parking untenable.

       Let's talk about all those Kittelson plots that show the 1541 available space line way, way above
       the lines showing spaces actually used. Creepy, not just because the 1541 includes the 300-
       space Seawall Drive parking lot that the city usually keeps closed. Mostly creepy because it
       sounds like a scam-too-good-to-be-true.

       I see the latest draft shows 300 spaces removed from the available space line to reflect the
       exclusion of the Seawall Drive parking lot. That's progress, but it's not nearly enough. Keep
       going, exclude all the lots that are just too far away from the South Cove to be useful. Spinnaker
       Way, Spinnaker Way Lot, D & E lots are all useless to recreational users of the South Cove. Asa,
       all of the slip holders parking lots (J&K, L, what's left of M, 0 and F&G, and H&I) are shown as
       "Available Spaces" (fig 6), even though filling them up with ferry parking would lead to an
       exodus of slip holders (who need and pay for that parking) and a major financial crisis for the
       Marina.

       The Kittelson study describes a marina where patrons may need to park far from their desired
       destination, and then use wayfinding, shuttles, micromobility or walking to get where they
       actually want to go. This profoundly degrades the experience of spending time at the marina.
       Let's say I want to take my grandsons to Adventure Playground for an hour. I drive down there
       and park on Marina Boulevard. A shuttle is useless, as would be taking a bus to the marina-
       the kids have to be in their car seats, and they usually have drinks, snacks and a lot of other
       stuff. How long does it take to get parked and walk/micro-mobility/uber/whatever down to
       Adventure Playground? And what happens when you forgot your grandson's warm jacket in the
       car, do you have to go all the way back to grab it?

       The day now centers around parking logistics rather than making stuff and zip-lining at
       Adventure Playground. How can you say that the Ferry project has not usurped the parking-
       and the happiness-of these recreational users?

The 315-space Seawall Drive lot was closed in 2018 to deal with a homeless RV encampment,
and the city has kept it mostly closed ever since. At this point, that's seven years and counting of
parking in the marina being compromised. This has been a horrendous breach of the city's
responsibility to maintain public access, and has significantly exacerbated parking problems in the

                                             2                                     05-April-2025 G. Stout
South Cove as well as undermined the city's credibility with the Marina recreational
communities. Perhaps the City thinks that closing the Seawall lot will make everyone forget that the lot
provided important recreational parking. We did not forget:

The Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project must plan for the following categories of parking
access that historically were provided by the Seawall Drive lot:

   1. Some of this lot-I would guess 50 spaces-used to provide parking for families wanting to
       carry in supplies to picnic or barbecue at Shorebird Park. I don't have data, but I believe that
       such picnics essentially stopped in Shorebird Park when the Seawall Drive lot was closed.

   2. More spaces-again I would guess about 50 spaces-were used by people fishing off the pier
       before it was closed in 2015. There needs to be parking in the plan for these people, many of
       whom need to bring tackle and take fish back home, not ideal for bike or bus travel.

   3. Going back in time, perhaps 100 spaces were used by Hs Lordships restaurant, and some spaces
       will be needed for a new restaurant if it is to be successful. Food trucks also need nearby
       parking.

   4. Another block of spaces {10 or 20?) was used by people launching from Lordships Cove. If there
       is a good launch put in at the Cove, it will need, say, 50 spaces, more if the South Basin is not
       dredged.

   5. It was a very important overflow lot for the other South Cove parking lots, way closer than
       Marina Boulevard and about as close as Skates.

   This totals 250 spaces, maybe only 150 spaces if they stagger time-wise, are we thinking we could
   squeeze 150 more cars in the South Cove and Skates lots? I don't think so, not even close.

   Income and Paid Parking Paid parking is of course a key strategy to try to make the Ferry
   project parking work. But Kittelson's Intercept Study found that 16% of responses reported
   household incomes of less than $50,000 and 10% less than $25,000. Also, 30% of the respondents
   come to the marina "a few times a week". Let's say it's 3 times a week, 30 weeks a year, and a $10
   parking charge, that's 3 x 30 x $10 = $900 per year. On a $25,000 income, that's crazy! We should
   not allow the ferry project to force paid parking onto the Marina!

   License Plate Readers, Parking Permits, and Pay Kiosks Expensive infrastructure, useful if
   the Marina is to be turned into a big-league ferry terminal. Not so useful otherwise.

Parking-TOM Response for EIR April 05, 2025 G. Stout
Executive Summary
   •   The parking studies that have been reported do not provide a clear picture of recreational
       parking at the marina. Without a clear picture, good parking plans and a credible EIR are not
       possible. This needs to be fixed, and soon, if 2025 is going to provide usable data.
   •   From the data and experience that we do have, it does seem clear that existing recreational
       parking is often maxed out without the ferry.
   •   The marina is currently used by low-income patrons for whom paid parking would be
       problematic. Can parking management without paid parking be made to work? Paid parking
       has a negative impact.
   •   The Kittelson study describes a marina where patrons may need to park far from their desired
       destination, and then use wayfinding, shuttles, micromobility or walking to get where they
       actually want to go. This profoundly degrades the experience of spending time at the marina,
       and should be counted as a negative impact with no obvious mitigation in the EIR.
   •   If every parking lot is completely full of parked cars, the marina will be uglier than it is now.
   •   What can families with small children do when the only available parking is in parking lots
       distant from where they want to take their families?
   •   Were attempts made to persuade Genentech to get their ferry riders not to park in the South
       Cove parking lots?
   •   Dynamic Management: if this is actually a strategy, who within the city will advocate for
       keeping recreational parking available?

Waterfront Monitors Parking Counts Referring to the Kittleson study attached to the PRW meeting
agenda, what is the availability of recreational parking in and around the South Cove? Dunno, darn it-
the Kittelson study still does not have believable answers to this crucial question. Page 22/129: "The
City of Berkeley Waterfront Monitors have been consistently collecting daily parking counts at the
Waterfront since May 2021. The data is collected by counting the number of occupied spaces at each
lot at 10 am and 8 pm, with the results recorded on a paper survey form that is later entered into a
spreadsheet maintained by Waterfront staff."

"Limitations: The data may not reflect peak utilization which could occur outside of the hours of 10 am
and 8 pm. In Spring, 2024, staff began collecting data at additional time points (2 pm and 4 pm), which
was not used for this study due to the comparatively limited number of data points"

Kittelson's 10 am-8pm data Limitations caveat casts doubt on most of the report. In the November 18,
2024 Council Worksession, the WSP was paused to conduct a parking study to determine existing



                                            1                                     05-April-2025 G. Stout
conditions for parking. Unfortunately, the Kittelson study still relies on the 10 am- 8pm data (Figure
10). The WSP needs to remain paused until a credible parking study is conducted.

I am placing my exploration of the data question in Appendix A at the end of this document, because
there are other issues I also want to cover:

Negotiate with WETA Why, oh why does Berkeley accept as a constraint whatever ridership goal
WETA proposes? Berkeley is the entity with the obligation to BCDC to not allow ferries to encroach
upon recreational use. Why are we not telling WETA that they must stop selling ferry tickets when
parking overwhelms the marina? Isn't that the way around it ought to be? If we told WETA they could
have 300 passengers per day, the marina might remain a great park.

The Intercept Survey has this:

       •   16% (63 people) reported having cancelled their visit to the waterfront because they could
           not find a parking space. That is a disaster, especially if you have a car full of kids!

   This is clear evidence that there is in fact not sufficient parking available.

       •   16% of responses reported household incomes of less than $50,000
       •   10%, less than $25,000

Unless we want the marina to be a park just for Berkeley's well-heeled, we should not implement paid
parking here. The ferry riders will have those well-paying jobs that the Pier-Ferry project touted in
selling itself to the City Council, so they should have much higher incomes than many of the
recreational marina patrons. Ferry riders will be able to afford "penalty" tickets, recreational patrons
may not.

Recreational Users are in a Losing Position They arrive late, when most of the parking lots have
already been scouted by the ferry and charter boat riders. And many recreational patrons don't have
the income for normal paid parking or the occasional expensive "oops-missed the time limit" tickets.
Bad deal for them, we shouldn't let it happen.

Families can't readily move from one parking lot to another Say your minivan full of kids
can't find a parking space in the West Cove lot to go to Adventure Playground. Are you going to park
up on Marina Boulevard and somehow walk, shuttle, bike, or Uber your kids back to Adventure
Playground?

Liza,
This is a somewhat different set of considerations for the WETA ferry dock location, please also include
it with the EIR scoping inputs.
Thanks!
Gordon
   Wind, Waves, and Lee Shore at the WETA Ferry Dock Location




This is a still picture from a video (attached, I suggest you watch it) of conditions in Berkeley's
south sailing basin with a strong south wind blowing directly across the south-facing
seawall. Note the reflected waves, and the spray overtopping the seawall. With a strong
north wind, the proposed north-facing WETA dock would probably look something like the
video, with waves breaking over the dock and soaking anyone on it.

North and South Winds
Strong North and South wind events happen several times a year on the Bay. The figure below
shows the Sword configuration presented at Workshop #2. Wave protection looks good for the
predominant west-to-southwest wind directions, but strong North to Northwest wind and waves
would hit the WETA docks with full force, with waves overtopping the docks much like the
waves in the video. Protecting the WETA docks against waves coming from the north is not at
all easy because a breakwater cannot be placed within or directly upwind of the ferry turning
basin. This is a serious problem for a dock in this location, which probably would mean
cancelling ferry service on days with north winds above a certain threshold.

For a South wind, the 'Sword' hilt forms (as labeled in the figure) a Protected Berthing Position,
but if there is no wave attenuation for the Lower Wave Condition berth, waves would probably
overtop the float in full view of passengers waiting in line for the ferry in the Protected Berthing
Position. Entertaining, perhaps, but not confidence-inspiring. Wave attenuation for south wind
storms needs to be present for both the Lower Wave Condition berth and the Protected Berthing
Position.




                                                  1
Nearby Lee Shore
In the usual westerly summer winds, an inbound ferry will come downwind to a position north of
the ferry's berth, then make a 180° turn in the "Ferry Turning Basin" so it ends up pointed
upwind when docked. But the summer winds are often well above 25 mph, and the waves can be
substantial, a bit like those in the picture above. The 180° turn would at the very least give the
ferry captains a good chance to demonstrate their skill.
There is a significant hazard here, however: the ferry turning basin is just a few boat lengths
upwind of both the rocky shore and the Skates restaurant. If a ferry were to lose power or
steering control just before the 180° turn, it would not take long for the ferry's eastward motion,
helped by a strong summer wind, to carry it down to the shore. It might ground on the rocks,
which would be dangerous, or collide with the Skates restaurant, which would be very dangerous
indeed. Skates is built on tall, slender pilings (see below) and might not survive a collision with
a 135-foot-long ferry, especially if the ferry were to drift under the restaurant. The chance of
injury in such an accident would be significant.

Perhaps after a power loss there would be time and room to set an anchor, perhaps not-an
anchor would have to be dropped almost immediately after loss of power to have a chance of
stopping the ferry in time. For the crew to deal with such a situation, they must have appropriate
equipment and rigorous training in how to use it, very much like the training aircraft pilots
receive for engine failures during takeoffs.




                                                 2
With well-maintained ferries, this kind of power loss should be a very rare event. Given the
potential hazard involved, though, I think this is a safety issue that needs to be carefully
evaluated for this site.

WETA's new Treasure Island ferry dock also has a windy location and a close lee shore-and,
for what it's worth, a breakwater to protect against north winds and waves. Perhaps WETA has
investigated this problem. If so, they should share their work.




Wind and Wave Modeling
In 2018, the city commissioned a study by GHD, Small Scale Ferry Terminal FS Berkeley
Municipal Pier_DRAFTpdf, that should have helped with the design of the pier and the
identification of the lee shore problem. Unfortunately, the study used wind data from NOAA's
Alameda Station, a far less windy location than the Berkeley Marina, so the wave modeling was
for 12 mph west wind and was therefore useless (see pages iii, 24, and 25). If the Berkeley Pier
docking site is to be used, a wind and wave study should be completed using real-world data,
probably obtainable from iWindsurf, which has several nearby wind sensors and archives of
wind strength/direction data. This data should allow modeling wave action for all wind
directions, and so guide the design of wave protection for the ferry docks. Modeling should
include prediction of silting resulting from candidate breakwater designs.




                                                3
Pier Structure Design
The design of the pier structure also needs consideration: the design chosen has monopile bents
along the pier centerline, unlike the existing pier which has its pilings along the north and south
pier edges.




     0A   SECTION
          IQ.&.Cllr'- 14 '
                                                     ©       SECTION
                                                             ,u.   llf"orr


Figure 8 - Repl:acement Pier Concept using Monopile Bents




                                                     cc:o    CA
                                                     f'RESTI,fS16JI



      @!~,.                                           ®~S=E~~=·~=.-- - - - - - -
 figure 9 - Repl:acement Pier Concept using Two Concrete Pile Bents


This design choice has safety implications: the centerline structure makes it much more likely
that a boat that gets blown against the pier will end up under the pier deck (see picture below of a
boat blown under the San Mateo bridge in 2009). Widening the stance of the two concrete pile
bents and keeping the along-pier pile spacing low would provide better protection against a boat
ending up under the pier.
(Figures above from study by GHD, Small Scale Ferry Terminal FS Berkeley Municipal
Pier_DRAFTpdf, pages 11 and 12.)




                                                 4
                                                                                         Michael Macor / The Chronicle

Picture/story:
https://www .sfgate.com/bayarea/article/Crews-to-move-boat-stuck-at-San-Mateo-Bridge-3 I 65070.php#photo-2297 687

In addition to the safety implications, the location of the piles has implications for fishing from
the pier, since the pilings and the biomass that attaches to them are part of the food chain of fish
and crabs. The current pier construction allows fishing directly adjacent to the pier support
pilings, which, if I remember from long ago, gets more bites. This should be looked into before
finalizing the design. Keeping part of the underwater structure of the old pier should also be
considered.

Dredge the North Marina Entrance
As a person who goes in and out of the marina under sail, I would choose to use the north harbor
entrance at times when both ferries and fishing charter boats are likely to be using the south
entrance. Therefore, I think that the ferry project should undertake the dredging of the north
harbor entrance as well as the south one, so that boats leaving and entering the marina have the
opportunity to avoid possible congestion near the ferry dock.
