Subject: Scoping comments for proposed pier ferry project EIR

Dear Ms. McNulty:

The following are my comments on the NOP. I incorporate with these new comments my
letter of March 18, 2025, on the Kittelson report, which points out in detail the inadequacy
of that report to support an EIR. Also incorporated and attached are two e-mails to you,
pointing out that the scope of study for Kittelson was not adequate, and identifying
problems with the May 7, 2025, Kittelson addendum. I have submitted a Public Records
Act request to gain access to the underlying data used in the May 7, 2025, addendum, and
reserve the right to augment my comments about that report when I have been provided
with the information I requested.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

For over forty years the courts have consistently held that an accurate and stable project
description is a bedrock requirement of CEQA-the sine qua non (that without which there
is nothing) of an adequate CEQA document:
       Only through an accurate view of the project may affected outsiders and
       public decision-makers balance the proposal's benefit against its
       environmental cost, consider mitigation measures, assess the advantage of
       terminating the proposal (i.e., the "no project" alternative) and weigh other
       alternatives in the balance. An accurate, stable and finite project description
       is the sine qua non of an informative and legally sufficient EIR.

(Inyo, supra, 71 Cal.App.3d at 192-93.)

The ability of informed citizens to participate in environmental review is a key component of
CEQA. (Washoe, supra, 17 Cal.App.5th at 285 ["Informed public participation is essential
to environmental review under CEQA."]; Inyo, supra, 71 Cal.App.3d at 192 ["The EIR
process facilitates CEQA's policy of supplying citizen input."].) Through the EIR process,
CEQA "provide[s] public agencies and the public in general with detailed information about
the effect which a proposed project is likely to have on the environment." (Washoe, supra,
17 Cal.App.5th at 286 [quoting Pub. Res. Code§ 21061 ].)
                                                 2


In Washoe, the court evaluated a DEIR prepared by the California Department of Parks and
Recreation which described five different alternatives for a project, including an existing
18-hole golf course, to reduce sediment discharge from the Upper Truckee River into Lake
Tahoe. (Washoe, supra, 17 Cal.App.5th at 283.) The DEIR did not identify a preferred
alternative but instead proposed that, after comments had been received on the DEIR, the
Department would identify the preferred alternative in the FEIR to" determine which
alternative or combinations of features from multiple alternatives will become the
preferred alternative." {Id . at 283.) In the FEIR, the Department identified "[a] refined
version of Alternative 2" as the preferred alternative. The Department subsequently
certified the FEIR. (Id. at 283-84.) The petitioners sought to set aside the approval of the
project because, inter alia , the DEIR did not contain an "accurate, stable and finite" project
description. (Id. at 287.)

A few examples should demonstrate this problem here. First, the NOP acknowledges that
"the City may choose not to implement these [recreational improvements] {page 3).
Second, the city's proposal for ferry parking, and for management of conflicts with
recreational parking, continues to change. Some of the material on the city web site calls
for a 250-space parking lot for ferry parking. But one of the exhibits submitted to BCDC for
review by the Design Review Board now designates that area, part of the bay that was filled
for recreational use, as a paid parking lot, apparently for ferry riders. Yet another exhibit
now shows the addition of 11 O spaces to the existing parking lot-without clarifying the
number of spaces proposed for ferry parkers. Is it 250, as most documents state, or is it
approaching the 400 spaces that WETA sought in 2008? An accurate depiction of the area
and its proposed future use was not included in the NOP. That in turn has a direct effect on
the usurpation of parking now used for recreational access by swimmers, wingers,
windsurfers, and anglers.

As of May 7, Berkeley has proposed two additional changes in the project description.
Berkeley circulated an addendum to the Kittelson study which now proposes that the
Skates/N Lot" and Marina Boulevard be used as overflow lots. Few details of those new
proposals are available. As part of the regular meeting of the Parks, Recreation and
Waterfront Commission, the city is now also proposing to start charging for parking at the
marina. It is impossible to develop a defensible EIR when the project description keeps
changing. The problems with these specific proposals will be discussed below.


SUBSTANTIAL EVIDENCE/ENVIRONMENTAL SETTING

Section 15064{f){5) of the CEQA Guidelines requires that information used in an EIR shall
not include "... speculation, ... or evidence that is not credible ..." Instead, it requires that
"Substantial evidence shall include facts, reasonable assumptions predicated upon
facts, and expert opinion supported by facts."
                                              3


In many of the background documents used to develop the current project description and
public presentation, Berkeley has ignored readily available substantial evidence and has
instead relied upon expert opinion that depends on modeling rather than facts about the
current ferry operations by WETA and by Berkeley lessees. Readily available information
about parking utilization, developed nearly a year ago, was not used in developing the
Kittelson parking report. That information, and details about the parking counts that
Kittelson was told to rely on, was only obtained through Public Records Act requests. Now
the city has released an addendum to the Kittelson report. However, that addendum does
not reveal the underlying data nor does that addendum seem to use the few data points
where parking counts were taken during the peak hours of the summer recreational
season. Conclusions provided with no underlying analysis that provides the necessary
data and links it to the reasoning fails the substantial evidence test. My e-mail to Liza
McNulty explaining the problems with the addendum is attached and incorporated by
reference.

The city must develop an environmental setting section for the document (Guidelines
Section 15125) that "normally constitute{s} the baseline physical conditions ..." Such a
baseline must include enough information about existing recreational use, existing parking
patterns, existing bicycle use, and existing ridership on the Genentech Ferry, to allow
analysis of the impacts of the proposed project on recreation and on consistency with
Berkeley and BCDC policies and other regulatory and planning standards.

RIDERSHIP PROJECTIONS

The NOP and supporting documentation on the city web site do not use substantial
evidence or consistent information to develop realistic projections of ridership. Available
information from the ferry operations that have operated in Berkeley since 2016 and from
similar WETA ferry routes is ignored, and speculative models are used. Even then, the
modeling information is used selectively and inconsistently without careful explanation.

Realistic projections, based on substantial evidence not speculation, are a necessary
element of any project description for preparing an EIR. Realistic ridership projections in
turn drive both impact analysis and questions of feasibility as a term of art under both the
California Environmental Quality Act and the McAteer-Petris Act. Realistic analysis, and its
implications for taxpayer cost and continued recreation are also fundamental issues for
Berkeley voters. Substantially more work needs to be done, and information from existing
efforts needs to be revealed.

Berkeley has approved three different small ferry operations, starting in November of 2016.
The city did not go through any public process in approving the first two ferry leases to Prop
SF and Tide line, considering the implications of the BCDC Bay Plan policies regarding
ferries, or coordinate that effort with BCDC. Riders began parking in the recreational
parking lot that had been improved with public funds and was subject to continued BCDC
jurisdiction, usurping recreational parking, in conflict with Bay Plan policies. An
                                              4


indeterminate number of riders of the Genentech ferry still park in those lots and the city
refuses to document that use. When I visited the marina May 15, 2025, by bicycle at 9:15
am, at least ten cars that appeared to be ferry riders were parked in the South Basin East
lot, and only one bicycle was visible in the bike lockers next to the bait shop. Other ferry
users were parked in the South basin West lot.

The City Manager informed the Council about the initiation of ferry service in a
memorandum dated November 21, 2016, that stated:

       Six months into the pilot program, the City will begin an RFP process that
       should result in a more long-term agreement ... As part of this process, the
       City will hire a parking and traffic engineer to study Waterfront use patterns
       and impacts and will provide more permanent recommendations for all
       Waterfront parking lots. (emphasis added)

The city derived revenue from a per passenger fee of $1, as noted in the November 16
memorandum. Yet the city has not used this data to develop the current proposal or
published a final report on the results of the six-month pilot project. I obtained some of the
records of ridership, which seem to be reported simply as revenue. If the financial records
provided to me are accurate and complete, Tideline's best month seems to have been May
23, 2017, to June 20, 2017, with 1085 passengers. That's about 54 passengers per day on
average, which as we know, mostly drove and parked their cars primarily in the South Basin
recreational lots, taking up about 25% of the parking spaces.

Because there is substantial price elasticity in the demand for ferry services, and in the net
requirement for public subsidy, the discussion of ridership projections must be accurate,
stable, and supported by substantial evidence that reflects an understanding of price
elasticity and its effect on ridership. The assumptions about pricing and the impact on
demand must be transparent and must not change. There are multiple citations on WETA's
web site and in WETA Board packets acknowledging price elasticity. During the pandemic,
WETA lowered the fees for ferry passengers well below their 40% fare box recovery policy to
compete with BART, with adult fares as low as $4. 70; before the pandemic the standard
adult fare from Alameda and Oakland was $7.20. That cheaper fare resulted in more
ridership-but decreased operational revenues to an unsustainable level. This is prima
facie evidence that price elasticity is a major factor in demand for ferry services and cannot
be ignored.

WETA staff and board are aware that raising costs for riders, either fares or parking charges,
could affect demand. The WETA Board is considering an MOU with Alameda since
Alameda is planning to begin charging for parking. That MOU provides as a stipulation:
"Ensure paid parking is implemented such that ridership at the Alameda ferry terminals is
not considerably impacted."
                                              5


The subsidies from Regional Measure 3 are not sufficient to cover the shortfall in
operational expenses with such a low fare. The May 8, 2025, agenda packet for the WETA
Board reports that the current operating revenue is not sufficient to sustain the existing
network. (page 107) It further reports that an additional $55 million in revenue would be
needed over 12 years to support adding a Berkeley route. That is more than $4 million a
year. In the last few years WETA has used Federal pandemic relief funding to lower the
fares; those funds have been exhausted. The shortfall in fare box revenue covered by those
funds was well above the available operational subsidy in Regional Measure 3. Total
operational costs for 2022 were $62 million, with only $12 million secured by fares.
Regional Measure 3 only provides $35 million in funding to subsidize fares. Currently, cost
recovery from such lowered fares is well under the 40% cost recovery policy on all routes,
with the overall system only generating 22% of its revenue from fares and Richmond only
generating 13%. (May 8, 2025, WETA Board Agenda packet).

Increasing fares directly to meet operating costs, or indirectly to charge for parking at the
proposed new terminal, is certain to reduce demand for ferries. The nature of reduced
demand due to price elasticity needs to be established and used in considerations of
feasibility. Such information is substantial evidence that cannot be ignored or replaced by
speculation based on models. The potential effect of charging for parking is quite
substantial. Earlier reports by Nelson/Nygaard estimated the cost of parking management
at $550,000. The city is currently entertaining a substantially more comprehensive and
expensive set of measures but has not provided a cost estimate. If the cost to effectively
manage parking were to be on the order of $1,000,000, and that cost were to be recovered
by parking fees, the daily parking fee could be as high as $16 per day. (250 parking spaces
times 250 weekdays, excluding holidays, = 62,500 days. $1,000,000/62,500 parking days=
$16 per day.) This nearly triples the cost of a round-trip ferry ride and obviously would
reduce demand. Even the lower cost estimate made in earlier studies would result in a
parking fee above $8 per day unless parking is actively subsidized by Berkeley or WETA, or
by recreational users as the city is currently considering. To be sure, if ridership does not
materialize, or if riders successfully park in free recreational areas, the city or WETA would
have to cover even more of the annual operational costs.

The prototype small ferry operations are relevant because Tide line and PROP SF charged
higher fares than Berkeley is anticipating for a WETA ferry, and Tideline currently operates a
ferry which is funded largely, if not completely, by Genentech. That information is readily
available, substantial information that needs to be utilized in determining ridership and the
impact of increased costs, either fares or parking fees, on demand. Since actual ridership
during the last decade seems to be well below that projected by models, unless heavily
subsidized, that ridership pattern provides substantial information about the impact of
pricing on demand and must be revealed and used in preparation of an EIR. At present,
Berkeley and WETA are projecting ridership using models and do not include the lessons of
existing operations, the two small ferry operators, or the impact of price increases. Ten
years after approval of a pilot project intended to develop information about the feasibility
                                               6


of ferry operations at Berkeley, the city has not completed and made public any analysis of
the lessons learned.

Beyond the problems with modeled demand that does not reflect price elasticity or recent
experience, the city is using an outdated business plan and the year 2040 to minimize the
potential impact of ridership on recreational use. The city is projecting only 915 departing
passengers from Berkeley, based on a 2022 WETA business plan. (Again, inconsistent
projections are used, with the Kittelson parking study using yet a different number.) This is
different from the plans presented in WETA's update of their long-term plan for 2050, dated
April 12, 2023. On Page 24, in Table 11, it provides 4 different ridership forecasts for the
proposed Berkeley service. The "Steady as it goes" scenario forecasts a ridership of
2,500. The "Throttle Back" scenario forecasts a ridership of 1,800. The "Chart New
Course" scenario forecasts a ridership of 4,000. The "Tack to the Wind" scenario forecasts
a ridership of 2,600. (Ridership as used in these documents represents two-way travel, so
departures are half of that, ranging from 900 to 2000.) The ferry system proposed has even
greater capacity, offering 400 seat vessels and 8 morning departures, or a capacity of 3200
departing passengers. All these different projections need to be evaluated in the EIR, and if
necessary, enforceable mitigation measures must be included to prevent significant
adverse impacts, namely usurping recreational parking.

The city cannot claim that the baseline for purposes of all EIR considerations is the level of
recreation and associated parking during 2025. The city has failed to maintain recreational
facilities, often after accepting grants to build those facilities, and closed parking lots that
would support greater recreational access if they were not closed. The city has closed the
pier, the nearby parking lot, the east dock in the South Basin, and H's Lordships restaurant.
All of those supported substantial recreational use and required parking. Allowing those
facilities to deteriorate and then claiming that their former use should not be considered
the baseline is improper. The city should not be allowed to artificially distort the baseline to
make usage appear to be artificially low. For example, in Save Our Peninsula, supra, 87
Cal.App.4th 99, 124-125, the court held that the city could not rely on a water usage
baseline that was artificially decreased only months prior to the release of the CEQA
document. Instead, the baseline was required to be the actual average levels of historic
levels of usage from past years. The city rather should use the BCDC standard and
analyze the existing and future recreational needs, much of which is impossible now
because of the city's deliberate neglect. For example, in the case of fluctuating usage, it is
appropriate to use the highest level of actual usage from the past as the baseline. For
example, in the case of Fairview Neighbors v. Cnty. of Ventura (1999) (70 Cal. App. 4th 238,
242) the court allowed traffic numbers occurring when the mine operated at peak capacity
pursuant to the prior CUP to be the "baseline," since mine operations were widely variable
depending on market factors. The peak capacity (over 81 Otruck trips) was actually
achieved in years prior, so it was not a mere hypothetical situation. The court rejected the
appellant's claim that actual existing traffic numbers (at the time of the EIR) had to be used.
Thus, in the situation fluctuating usage, a description of baseline environmental setting
may reasonably include the area's established levels of prior use. (San Joaquin Raptor
                                              7


Rescue Ctr. v. Cnty. of Merced (2007) 149 Cal. App. 4th 645, 658.) Here, with a recreational
resource that receives its highest use in the summer when different recreational programs
and camps take place in the south basin, and where BCDC's Bay Plan policies specifically
state that ferry parking cannot usurp recreational parking or displace existing or future
recreational needs, the intent to protect peak summer activities is clear.

PIECEMEALING

CEQA defines a "project" broadly, as the whole of project, including future and related
projects. CEQA mandates "that environmental considerations do not become submerged
by chopping a large project into many little ones -- each with a minimal potential impact on
the environment - which cumulatively may have disastrous consequences." (Bozung v.
LAFCO, 13 Cal.3d 263, 283-84 (1975); City of Santee v. County of San Diego, 214
Cal.App.3d 1438, 1452 (1989).) Before undertaking a project, the lead agency must assess
the environmental impacts of all reasonably foreseeable phases of a project and a public
agency may not segment a large project into two or more smaller projects in order to mask
serious environmental consequences. As the Court of Appeal stated:

       "The CEQA process is intended to be a careful examination, fully open to the public,
       of the environmental consequences of a given project, covering the entire project,
       from start to finish ... the purpose of CEQA is not to generate paper, but to compel
       government at all levels to make decisions with environmental consequences in
       mind." (Natural Resources Defense Council v. City of Los Angeles, 103 Cal.App.4th
       268 (2002).)

Similarly, an initial study must consider the "whole of an action." 14 Cal. Code Regs.§
15378(a). That means:

       "[T]he environmental review accompanying the first discretionary approval must
       evaluate the impacts of the ultimate development authorized by that approval. ...
       Even though further discretionary approvals may be required before development
       can occur, the agency's environmental review must extend to the development
       envisioned by the initial approvals. It is irrelevant that the development may not
       receive all necessary entitlements or may not be built. Piecemeal environmental
       review that ignores the environmental impacts of the end result will not be
       permitted."

See Kostka, et al., Practice Under the California Environmental Quality Act, § 6.52, p. 298.

Berkeley and WETA are proposing to prepare an EIR on a ferry terminal on land filled for
recreational purposes. Under the current city Waterfront Plan, which was adopted in 2003,
that area is not designated as a ferry terminal. As discussed below, that plan inconsistency
itself creates a significant impact under CEQA. The city is preparing a revision to that plan,
now titled the "Waterfront Specific Plan", but has not completed that plan or prepared any
                                              8


environmental documents that cover the whole of the waterfront. The city has jurisdiction
over all the filled land, and the marina basin west of the East Shore State Park, this area,
the marina basin and adjacent land, and Cesar Chavez Park. The current draft of the WSP
is considering development scenarios that could triple the level of development in the
marina, as well as designate land for a ferry terminal.

The city takes the position, established in a memorandum to the Council on November 18,
2024, titled "Update of the Waterfront Specific Plan for the Berkeley Public Tidelands Area",
that:

       ...the Pier Ferry Project does not depend on adoption of the WSP to occur
       [and] the upcoming Pier Ferry public process will precede the drafting of the
       CEQA document [for the WSP]

With no adopted plan that designates this site for a ferry terminal, and with a plan under
preparation that covers this site and could allow a tripling of development on the city land, I
believe this conclusion is incorrect. The latest changes proposed by city staff, use of the
Skates/N lot and Marina Boulevard for parking, and instituting parking fees throughout the
waterfront, make it even clearer that the current ferry project does not have independent
utility. It apparently depends on land under consideration for other uses in the WSP, and
revenues generated by areas covered by the WSP. The update of the WSP is clearly a
"reasonably foreseeable future" action that is necessary for the approval of the Ferry
Terminal Project. Redesignation of the land in question, and analysis of the related
projects that are under consideration, is necessary to avoid improper piecemealing under
CEQA. Independent utility alone is not sufficient to absolve the city of its responsibility to
evaluate the whole of the project, which can clearly be seen as the redevelopment of the
entire waterfront.

There are similar piecemealing concerns with the proposal, presented to the Parks,
Recreation, and Waterfront Commission on May 14, 2025, to begin charging for parking.
Berkeley has long announced its plans to control use at the marina in various planning and
policy documents, as long ago as 2016 {see discussion of ridership projections.) Instituting
parking fees was a strategy under consideration in the WSP and its predecessor effort and
is intended to limit travel to this regional park of State Tidelands by automobile. For
example, in a February 16, 2021, work session memo to the Council, staff stated: "Paid
parking at various locations at the Waterfront could generate additional revenue for the
City's Marina Fund, while simultaneously dis-incentivizing car-based traffic to the
Waterfront."

The Parking and Mobility Framework, January 2022, by Nelson/Nygaard included an
extensive discussion of paid parking, beginning with: "Paid parking is an effective tool for
managing demand and turnover in the most convenient, high-demand parking spaces."
and:
                                              9


   •   Paid parking must be implemented as part of a Waterfront-wide parking
       strategy to avoid spillover impacts on free or unregulated parking nearby.
   •   Targeting parking fees to specific users {such as ferry commuters) is potentially
       challenging, and should be avoided if possible. Such a strategy is difficult to enforce
       and may require creating physical barriers for cars that can hinder flexible shared
       parking approaches.
   •   Pricing can and should reflect demand and convenience. The most centrally located
       "premium" spaces could have a higher hourly price, while "value" spaces in more
       distant underutilized lots could be cheaper or free.
   •    A value/premium parking system should be supported with convenient
       pickup/drop-off zones {PUDO) that allow people to load and unload gear and
       equipment close to their destination before parking a bit further away.
   •    Recommendation for the BMASP: Include a comprehensive {not ferry-only)
       demand-based pricing strategy in the full build-out scenario. Identify all locations in
       the Waterfront where demand-based pricing may be appropriate.

Given these clear and repeated statements of intent, it can readily be seen that neither the
proposal for a pier-ferry project that depends on land designated for additional commercial
use in the WSP, nor the parking fees under consideration, are independent. The whole
WSP, including parking fees and the pier-ferry project, is simply one project under CEQA.

CUMULATIVE IMPACTS

If the city contends that the Ferry Terminal and the WSP are separate projects, rather than a
single piecemealed project, it still must analyze the two projects' cumulative impacts
because the WSP is a reasonably foreseeable future project. An EIR must discuss
significant cumulative impacts of reasonably foreseeable future project. {CEQA Guidelines
section 15130{a).) This requirement flows from CEQA section 21083, which requires a
finding that a project may have a significant effect on the environment if "the possible
effects of a project are individually limited but cumulatively considerable .... 'Cumulatively
considerable' means that the incremental effects of an individual project are considerable
when viewed in connection with the effects of past projects, the effects of other current
projects, and the effects of probable future projects." "Cumulative impacts" are defined as
"two or more individual effects which, when considered together, are considerable or
which compound or increase other environmental impacts." {CEQA Guidelines section
15355{a).) "[l]ndividual effects may be changes resulting from a single project or a number
of separate projects." {CEQA Guidelines section 15355{a).)

"The cumulative impact from several projects is the change in the environment which
results from the incremental impact of the project when added to other closely related
past, present, and reasonably foreseeable probable future projects. Cumulative impacts
can result from individually minor but collectively significant projects taking place over a
period of time." (Communities for a Better Environment v. Cal. Resources Agency ("CBE v.
                                              10


CRA"), (2002) 103 Cal.App.4th 98, 117.) A legally adequate cumulative impacts analysis
views a particular project over time and in conjunction with other related past, present, and
reasonably foreseeable probable future projects whose impacts might compound or
interrelate with those of the project at hand. "Cumulative impacts can result from
individually minor but collectively significant projects taking place over a period of time."
(CEQA Guidelines§ 15355(b).)

       As the COLI rt stated in CBE v. CRA, 103 Cal. App. 4th at 114:

       Cumulative impact analysis is necessary because the full environmental impact of
       a proposed project cannot be gauged in a vacuum. One of the most important
       environmental lessons that has been learned is that environmental damage often
       occurs incrementally from a variety of small sources. These sources appear
       insignificant when considered individually, but assume threatening dimensions
       when considered collectively with other sources with which they interact.

(Citations omitted).

For example, in Friends of Eel River v. Sonoma County Water Agency, (2003) 108 Cal. App.
4th 859, the court held that the EIR for a project that would divert water from the Eel River
had to consider the cumulative impacts of the project together with other past, present and
reasonably foreseeable future projects that also divert water from the same river system.
The court held that the EIR even had to disclose and analyze projects that were merely
proposed, but not yet approved. The court stated, CEQA requires "the Agency to consider
'past, present, and probable future projects producing related or cumulative impacts ... .'
(Guidelines, § 15130, subd. (b)(1 )(A).) The Agency must interpret this requirement in such a
way as to 'afford the fullest possible protection of the environment.'" (Id., at 867, 869.) The
court held that the failure of the EIR to analyze the impacts of the project together with
other proposed projects rendered the document invalid. "The absence of this analysis
makes the EIR an inadequate informational document.'' (Id., at 872.)

Thus, even if the city contends that the WSP is a separate project, it must still analyze its
impacts together with the Ferry Terminal Project and the proposed new parking fees in the
present EIR because the WSP project is a reasonably foreseeable future project that will
have significant cumulative impacts.

CONSISTENCY WITH ADOPTED PLANS AND STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS

Section 15125(d) of the CEQA Guidelines requires that:

       The EIR shall discuss any inconsistencies between the proposed project and
       the applicable general plans and regional plans ... including ... regional land
       use plans for the protection of ... San Francisco Bay...
                                              11


Where a local or regional policy of general applicability, such as an ordinance, is adopted in
order to avoid or mitigate environmental effects, a conflict with that policy in itself
indicates a potentially significant impact on the environment. (Pocket Protectors v.
Sacramento (2005) 124 Cal.App.4th 903; Georgetown Preservation Society v. County of El
Dorado (2018) 30 Cal.App.5th 358.) Indeed, any inconsistencies between a proposed
project and applicable plans must be discussed in an EIR. (14 CCR§ 15125(d); City of Long
Beach v. Los Angeles Unif. School Dist. (2009) 176 Cal. App. 4th 889,918; Friends of the Eel
Riverv. Sonoma CountyWaterAgency(2003) 108 Cal. App. 4th 859,874 (EIR inadequate
when Lead Agency failed to identify relationship of project to relevant local plans).) A
Project's inconsistencies with local plans and policies constitute significant impacts under
CEQA. (Endangered Habitats League, Inc. v. County of Orange (2005) 131 Cal.App.4th 777,
783-4, 32 Cal.Rptr.3d 177; see also, County of El Dorado v. Dept. of Transp. (2005) 133
Cal.App.4th 1376 (fact that a project may be consistent with a plan, such as an air plan,
does not necessarily mean that it does not have significant impacts).)

In the preceding discussion I established the inconsistency between this proposed project
and the current plan for the Waterfront. The EIR must also discuss the following plans:

   •   Bay Plan policies cited in previous letters protecting parking for existing and future
       recreational uses;
   •   Bay Plan policies covering dredging, particularly policy 2, that "the siting and design
       of the project will result in the minimal dredging volume necessary for the project"
   •   The Water Trail Act, now included in the Public Resources Code, "with the goals of
       improving access to, within, and around the bay"
   •   Berkeley Measure L, ORDINANCE NO. 5785-N.S., with the goal of protecting and
       funding existing parks, requiring a public election to allow any parks to be developed
       for other purposes, and with a definition that includes this property as public trust,
       to wit: "Public parks shall be defined as City of Berkeley parks, public school
       playgrounds or lands held in trust by a public entity, which have been formally
       dedicated to permanent recreational use by the City of Berkeley, and funded for
       recreational use by City of Berkeley public funds"

The two cited BCDC Bay Plan policies have are legal requirements. In addition, there are
several legal requirements that would apply to this proposed project, including:

   •   Section 404(b) of the Clean Water Act, which establishes policies and guidelines to
       avoid, minimize, and if necessary mitigate activities that would dredge or fill waters
       of the bay;
   •   The Porter-Cologne Act which similarly includes a role in 404(b) determinations and
       independent authority under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act
   •   Section 4(f) of the Transportation Act, codified now as Title 409 Section 303(c) that
       forbids use of parks and recreational areas for transportation facilities "unless there
       is no prudent and feasible alternative"
                                              12



These plan and policy inconsistencies are significant impacts that must be analyzed and
mitigated under CEQA.

ALTERNATIVES

A central element of CEQA is the consideration of environmentally superior alternatives.
The feasibility of alternatives arises at two junctures in the EIR process: "(1) in the
assessment of alternatives in the EIR; and (2) during the agency's later consideration of
whether to approve the project;" and "different factors come into play at each stage."
(California Native PlantSocietyv. City of Santa Cruz (2009) 177 Cal.App.4th 957,981
(CNPS), citing Mira Mar Mobile Community v. City of Oceanside (2004) 119 Cal.App.4th
477,489 (Mira Mar).) When selecting alternatives to analyze in an EIR, the standard is
whether the alternative is "potentially feasible" and would reduce potentially significant
impacts. (Mira Mar, supra, 119 Cal.App.4th at 489; Guidelines, § 15126.G(a).) In the second
project approval phase, the decision-maker evaluates whether alternatives are actually
feasible, and may reject alternatives on grounds of actual infeasibility even though the EIR
found them potentially feasible and analyzed them. (Watsonville Pilots Assn. v. City of
Watsonville (2010) 183 Cal.App.4th 1059, 1087 (Watsonville); Guidelines, § 15091 (a)(3).)

It is an abuse of discretion for an agency to exclude a potentially feasible alternative that
would substantially reduce significant impacts from analysis in the EIR simply because it
does not meet all project objectives. (Habitat & Watershed Caretakers v. City of Santa Cruz
(2013) 213 Cal.App.4th 1277, 1304 (Caretakers) ["limited-water alternative could not be
eliminated from consideration solely because it would impede to some extent the
attainment of the project's objectives"]; Watsonville, supra, 183 Cal.App.4th at 1087
[agency's refusal to analyze a reduced development alternative because it failed to meet
two of 12 project objectives was legal error].)

Since the inception of this effort, Berkeley and WETA have refused to consider alternative
locations and sizes for a ferry terminal that would not present conflicts with recreational
use of the filled land or require new dredging and fill. The policies and statutes cited in the
previous section require any EIR that would be used by a responsible agency, including the
Federal Transit Administration, consider alternatives. The existing filled areas on the north
and south sides of the marina basin represent reasonable alternatives that must be
discussed in sufficient detail to determine their feasibility. Currently, Hornblower yachts
are berthed near the Doubletree Hotel. That site, and a site close to the dry boat storage,
which could be used for parking, should be considered as alternatives. Increasing BART
capacity or improving access to BART within Berkeley should also be considered.

FEASIBILITY

Feasibility is a term of art that has a slightly different meaning under CEQA and some of the
related regulatory standards that the EIR must analyze. For the purposes of this EIR, it is
                                              13


essential that the criteria used to determine feasibility-of the project, the possible
alternatives, and the BCDC standard of maximum feasible public access consistent with
the project--be transparent. No such transparency exists at the NOP stage.

CEQA defines "feasible" as capable of being accomplished in a successful manner within a
reasonable period of time, taking into account economic, environmental, social and
technological factors. (Pub. Res. Code§ 21061.1.) The guidelines add "legal"
considerations as a fifth factor that must be taken into account when determining whether
a mitigation measure or project alternative is feasible. (CEQA Guidelines§ 15364.) Neither
the statute nor the guidelines provide any substantive insights on how to analyze the
economic feasibility of an alternative or measure. The court in San Franciscans Upholding
the Downtown Plan v. City and County of San Francisco (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 656, 694,
upheld an infeasibility finding based on analysis of costs, projected revenues, and
investment requirements.

The court in Burger v. County of Mendocino (1975) 45 Cal.App.3d 322, identified three
criteria that should be evaluated when determining whether a project alternative would be
economically feasible: (1) estimated income; (2) estimated expenditures; and (3)
estimated profitability. Implicit in the court's finding is the need to conduct a comparative
analysis, on the basis of each of these criteria, between the proposed project and project
alternatives or the proposed project with and without the recommended mitigation
measure to determine whether a particular alternative or measure would render the project
economically infeasible.

In Citizens of Goleta Valleyv. Board of Supervisors (1988) ("Goleta/") 197 Cal.App.3d 1167,
the court confirmed the use of the criteria identified by the Burger court, added additional
criteria. The Goleta I court set forth five criteria against which a proposed project and
project alternative can be compared. They include the following: (1) total estimated costs;
(2) total projected income; (3) total expenses; (4) the change in the per unit cost of a project
that results from a project alternative or mitigation measure; and (5) the economic benefits
of the project to the community and public at large. In San Franciscans Upholding the
Downtown Plan v. City & Cnty. of San Francisco (2002) 102 Cal. App. 4th 656, the court
applied the standard established in Goleta I to uphold the City's decision that the project
alternatives discussed in the EIR were not economically feasible. Specifically, the court
found that substantial evidence supported the City's conclusion that the project
alternatives discussed in the EIR were infeasible because the additional costs and lost
profitability that would result from each of the alternatives were sufficiently severe to
render them impractical. (San Franciscans, supra, p. 695.)

Cost estimates for the overall project were last presented in 2021 when the initial
"feasibility study" was published and cost estimates were prepared that estimated the
total project cost at $121. 7 million and Berkeley's share at $29 million. The project has
been under constant change since then, but the cost implications of those changes have
not been presented. To a close observer, it appears that the project has no current source
                                              14


of funding and feasibility depends entirely on a combination of Federal grants and an
increase in the sales tax for Bay area counties, which may be on the November 2026 ballot,
further increases in the Bay Bridge toll, funding by Berkeley from the general fund or a bond
measure, or some combination of those options. No firm source of funding from Berkeley
for either construction or maintenance, or firm budget for those costs, has been identified.
The documents that I have seen from WETA's web site only allocate a portion of the capital
costs of initial construction and indicate that WETA plans to fund no more than half of the
ongoing operational subsidy.

In any conventional sense of the word, a new ferry terminal is not feasible. As a matter of
fact, it is not even possible without a massive level of subsidy, which comes mostly from
people who will never ride a ferry. The budget proposed for WETA for their May 8, 2025,
Board meeting estimates an operational cost of $81 million. The budget anticipates
3,032,823 riders-an 18% increase over the current year, which may be overly optimistic. If
that budget is correct, each rider costs $26. 70. The only recovery from those who are lucky
enough to ride is a fare of $4. 70. The performance metrics in the same WETA Board agenda
packet acknowledge that fare only account for 22% of the costs. That packet also
acknowledges that even more subsidies will be required to establish a Berkeley route.
Those crossing the bay under the City's assumption, 915 riders departing Berkeley, is less
than 1% of the roughly 116,000 west bound daily crossings of the Bay Bridge.

The EIR must bridge the analytical gap in these uncertainties to be able to reach
defendable conclusions about feasibility in the EIR that will provide the necessary
information for responsible agencies. I think it is essential that the following questions be
answered:

   1. How much money has WETA reserved for a Berkeley Ferry Terminal?
   2. How has WETA allocated funds from Regional Measure 3 to the various other
      planned projects, for both capital and annual operational costs? Is there a shortfall
      in funding for the Berkeley terminal in either capital or operational costs? If so, what
      is the magnitude of that shortfall?
   3. What is the updated total project cost estimate, capital and annual, for the Berkeley
      terminal if the project goes forward?
   4. Have any sources for that funding been identified?
   5. What would the economic effect be if ridership is less than anticipated? What
      agency or agencies would be responsible for the revenue shortfall?

These all relate to the question of alternatives. Given the relatively small ridership of the
two small ferry operations that have ceased in the Berkeley marina, it seems possible, and
perhaps even likely, that less ridership would materialize. A smaller operation, using
existing marina facilities and the entrance channel, should be evaluated as a more feasible
and far less risky alternative.
                                               15


RECREATIONAL IMPACTS

With BCDC policies clearly protecting existing and future recreational users from having
access to the marina impeded because ferry riders have usurped recreational parking, a
detailed discussion of recreational impacts is required. Stakeholders have long informed
the city that a baseline of recreational use for parking lots that might be usurped by ferry
riders is required, but the city has failed to collect sufficient data during recreational
periods to establish a baseline. In addition to the Bay Plan policies that I have cited,
Section 15064{e) of the CEQA guidelines is directly on point. It states that:

       If a project would cause overcrowding of a public facility and the
       overcrowding causes an adverse effect on people, the overcrowding would
       be regarded as a significant effect.

Since over 90% of those currently using the marina report that they rely on driving, and that
many of the recreational activities involve transporting equipment that is used to recreate
on or near the water, parking is integral to recreational access. My letter dated March 18,
2025, which explains the flaws in the Kittelson report is incorporated into these comments.
Because of those flaws, the misuse of statistical data, and the exclusion of relevant data,
that report cannot be used to develop an adequate analysis of the recreational impacts.
Also incorporated is the e-mail thread wherein I made similar comments.

In addition to the effect of usurping parking, which continues due to passengers on the
Genentech ferry, construction of a solid seawall in the Bay will alter the recreational
environment for sailors and those using small craft. Such facilities are known to refract
and reflect waves and disrupt wind patterns. Those impacts need to be thoroughly
evaluated and mitigated. I have provided my GPS track from May 8, 2025, at the end of
these comments that shows a typical path back into the marina entrance channel that
might be affected by reflection of wind and waves from the proposed terminal and ferries.
That impact must be analyzed. A second GPS track of the Pegasus sailing ship is also
attached and labeled. The Pegasus takes Berkeley school children out onto the bay for
free, fulfilling part of Berkeley's mandate to provide recreational facilities at the marina for
those who don't own a boat. I contribute both my time and make donations to support that
access.

As noted by members of BCDC's Design Review Board on May 12, 2025, further engineering
analysis of the proposed sheet pile breakwater structure must be completed to assure that
an accurate footprint of that structure is used for analysis. The structure affords
substantially less wave protection than the breakwaters for Berkeley marina. Even those
breakwaters required modification; the sheet pile breakwater north of the rubble mound
breakwater was added because waves were penetrating the harbor and causing damage.
The proposal for locating the ferry terminal outside of the protected marina raises further
issues. It would directly occupy a part of the bay used for recreation; my GPS tracks show
common paths for return to the marina. A sheet-pile breakwater would reflect both waves
                                              16


and wind, creating turbulence. It would also refract waves, changing their pattern in
proximity to the entrance to the marina. These impacts must be thoroughly evaluated in
the EIR.

While the city might argue that recreational impacts and parking are not within the scope of
CEQA, that is incorrect. First, to the extent the proposed project conflicts with applicable
policies, that is a significant impact under CEQA. As discussed above, the project conflicts
with several applicable policies protecting recreational uses and related parking. Second,
to the extent that the project's impacts on recreational uses results in environmental
impacts, those impacts are within the scope of CEQA. For example, the lack of parking for
recreational uses may result in illegal parking, cars circling for parking (resulting in greater
vehicle emissions and higher vehicle miles travelled). In San Franciscans Upholding the
Downtown Plan v. City and County of San Francisco (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 656, the court
acknowledged that a project may have significant parking-related impacts requiring
analysis in an EIR if there are secondary environmental impacts resulting from the
projected parking deficits. Third, to the extent that the Ferry Terminal is economically
infeasible, as discussed above, it may contribute to urban blight and urban decay in the
area, which is an impact under CEQA. (Bakersfield Citizens for Local Control v. City of
Bakersfield (2004) 124 Cal.App.4th 1184.)

GREEN HOUSE GASES

The EIR must address the carbon emissions generated by ferry traffic for two reasons. First,
there is no guarantee that electric ferries will be acquired by WETA and used on a Berkeley
route; Berkeley does not have the authority to mandate that. Second, the source of
electricity for any ferries that are deployed will likely be at least partially derived from
sources that generate electricity with fossil fuels. For that reason, the efficiency of the
proposed ferries should be presented as BTU's per passenger mile and should be
compared to alternative ways to cross the bay-BART, bus, and automobile. (See, Bay Area
Air Quality Management District Guidelines for Analysis of Greenhouse Gas Impacts under
CEQA, available at: https://www.baaqmd.gov/~/media/files/planning-and-
research/ceqa/ceqa-guidelines-2022/ceqa-guidelines-chapter-6-project-climate-
impacts final-pdf.pdf?rev=ce3ba3fe9d39448f9c15bbabd8c36c7f &sc lang=en).

Berkeley staff have made many presentations claiming that this project would be a zero-
emission transportation project. That is not true. Generating the electricity for the ferry
would require some level of carbon-based generation, either directly or indirectly. Unless
the project includes enough local generation of electricity so that it does not replace other
renewable sources, it would increase energy requirements with the same carbon signature
as the average for electricity generation in Berkeley. Further, access to the ferry terminal
would primarily be by single-occupancy car, and driving to Berkeley marina rather than
shorter drives to BART would be likely to increase vehicle mileage and carbon signatures.
The EIR must consider all emissions associated with the project, not simply the power
source of the proposed ferries.
                                               17



The EIR must be clear about the commitment to electrification of ferries that would be
used if a terminal were ultimately developed. Under the existing MOU between WETA and
Berkeley, WETA, not Berkeley is responsible for procuring and operating ferries. On April
11, 2024, Seamus Murphy presented the "Draft Service Vision and Expansion Policy" to the
WETA Board. It stated:

       System expansion and enhancement projects will deploy Zero Emission
       Vessels (ZEV), if feasible. (emphasis added)

Berkeley has not prepared a revised cost estimate for the project, which has been changed
substantially since the feasibility study. At that time, the total project cost was estimated
to be $121. 7 million, with ferry vessels estimated to cost $18 million each for a total cost of
$36 million. (Feasibility study page 179) Since that time WETA has entered into contracts
to purchase two electric ferries for costs of about $38 million each, adding about $40
million to the cost of the project. For the most part, ferries, including the fuel cell ferry now
in use, have been funded by grants rather than WETA funds. Obtaining Federal grants for
alternative transportation modes may be a difficult challenge during the current
administration, and the "take" of park, open space, and areas of the recreational bay
triggers Section 4(f) of the Transportation Act. Moreover, an accurate analysis of the air
quality and carbon dioxide generation impacts of the proposed ferry system depends on
the power plants that would be used to power the vessels. The EIR must be clear about
whether Berkeley intends to pursue a ferry terminal if electric ferries turn out to be
infeasible. While Berkeley might elect not to participate in the proposed project if WETA
does not use electric ferries, it is not clear that Berkeley can require WETA to use electric
ferries. In any event, the true carbon signature, including the generation of electricity to
charge the batteries of any electric ferries, must be analyzed in the EIR.

ENFORCEABILITY

A public agency may not rely on mitigation measures of uncertain efficacy or feasibility.
(Kings County Farm Bureau v. City of Hanford (1990) 221 Cal.App.3d 692, 727 (finding
groundwater purchase agreement inadequate mitigation measure because no record
evidence existed that replacement water was available).) "Feasible" means capable of
being accomplished in a successful manner within a reasonable period of time, taking into
account economic, environmental, legal, social and technological factors. (14 CCR§
15364.) Mitigation measures must be fully enforceable through permit conditions,
agreements or other legally binding instruments. (14 CCR§ 15126.4(a)(2); See Woodward
Park Homeowners Assn., Inc. v. City of Fresno (2007) 150 Cal. App. 4th 683, 730 (project
proponent's agreement to a mitigation by itself is insufficient; mitigation measure must be
an enforceable requirement); California Clean Energy Committee v. City of Woodland
(2014) 225 Cal. App.4th 173, 195-96.)
                                               18


PARKING

While my March 25, 2025, letter provides a thorough discussion of the inadequacy of the
city's approach to establishing a baseline of recreational use that is protected under the
Bay Plan, it is important to reiterate a few points. First, the Bay Plan Policies protect not
merely the existing recreational uses on the date of the NOP, but historic and future uses.
The language provides in Recreational Policy 9:

       Ferry terminals may be allowed in waterfront park priority use areas and
       marinas and near fishing piers and launching lanes, provided the
       development and operations of the ferry facilities do not interfere with
       current or future park and recreational uses, and navigational safety can
       be assured. Terminal configuration and operation should not disrupt
       continuous shoreline access. Facilities provided for park and marina
       patrons, such as parking, should not be usurped by ferry patrons. Shared
       parking arrangements should be provided to minimize the amount of
       shoreline area needed for parking.

Berkeley has made no attempt to account for future park and recreational uses protected
by that policy.

I also want to reiterate the comments made by several members of the Design Review
Board that Berkeley needs to provide a baseline, or as they said, map, of current users.
Those comments made it clear that the time and location of recreational use, and the
availability of parking, were necessary to evaluate the project. I'll repeat here a critical
comment from my March letter:

       There are twelve different parking lots in the marina, and probably as many
       different recreational activities. Correct use of data, if sufficient relevant
       data were to be collected, would identify which parking lots are underutilized
       and when. That would be a valuable tool in determining whether ferry
       passengers could be accommodated without usurping existing recreational
       activities. The approach used in the Kittelson study improperly combines
       both different locations and different times. This destroys the statistical
       value that the data ...

The Kittelson addendum repeats these errors, now claiming that unimproved parking along
Marina Boulevard, nearly a half mile from the proposed terminal, would provide adequate
parking to prevent usurpation of parking. As noted earlier, unsubstantiated claims do not
constitute substantial evidence.

The EIR must establish a level of baseline recreational use, before the city closed the pier,
the East dock, and two parking lots. They must account for the geographic location of the
users, or map them, as the DRB has directed. The city must spend more than $27,000 for
                                               19


analysis of the geographic location and time of use of the various recreational activities
that are protected and stop trying to repurpose irrelevant parking data that it claims
provides the necessary analysis.

DREDGING

Before the BCDC Design Review Board, Berkeley unveiled a footprint for the turning basin
of the proposed terminal, but did not reveal the volume of dredging required, or the amount
of new fill that might be required. Both are essential, as is analysis of the Bay Plan and
LTMS polices that direct a careful study of alternatives that would minimize both new
dredging and fill. I'll repeat that policy here: "the siting and design of the project will result
in the minimal dredging volume necessary for the project"

The city also claimed that the new terminal would not require maintenance dredging. That
is not accurate. There is still ample suspended sediment in the bay to settle in deeper
areas, and the construction of breakwaters provides reduced wave energy so that the area
behind the breakwater becomes a settling basin for sediment. The city operates Berkeley
marina and is engaged in a dredging operation. The before and after bathymetry of the
entrance channel and other dredged areas will provide a baseline of sedimentation which
can be compared to the time since the area was last dredged. Further, the South Basin of
Berkeley marina was dredged as a source of material for construction of the area now
proposed for this ferry terminal. Berkeley recently completed a bathymetric study of the
area. These two prototypes can be used to establish a rate of sedimentation that can be
used to estimate sedimentation associated with the proposed terminal.

Very truly yours,


Jim McGrath

Comments on the Scope of the EIR

No "moving target: " The ferry terminal and service details must be
established prior to the EIR process. Specifically, the parking plan. This will
have a very large effect on the impacts to recreational access. The most
likely parking plan needs to be determined in detail before the EIR will have
any meaning.

No incremental approval: The EIR must consider the impacts of "full
build-out." WETA is on record as planning a service that will eventually
grow to include 8 departures of 400-passenger boats every weekday
morning. Assuming 50% passenger load, that's 1600 one -way passengers
every morning, and at the usual 0.6 cars per passenger, that's 960 cars.
Yet the current parking analysis assumes only 389 parking spaces are
needed. This must be reconciled before the EIR can proceed. It should not
be necessary to point out that 389 is a much smaller number than 960.
WETA needs to show a binding commitment to limit the level of service to
that which is considered for the EIR. If the service proves to be popular and
ridership and parking demands increase, WETA needs to commit to using
the known market elasticity (ferry fare pricing) to limit parking demand to
the level considered by the EIR.

Distance to parking: No half-mile walks without some reasonable
accommodations (shuttle bus, free e-bikes, etc.) The parking plan assumes
Marina Blvd parking area will provide overflow. The nearest Marina Blvd
parking spaces (at the south end) are 2400 feet from the pier entrance,
most of the spaces in that parking area are more than a half mile from the
pier.

Parking fees: The Marina is seriously considering a $1/hour fee for ALL
marina parking. This would increase cost to the passenger by
approximately 50% per round trip (assuming about $10 ferry fare each
way). Is the ferry still feasible at $1/hour parking fee?

Parking management: The parking pattern for a guest on a sailboat is
almost exactly the same as the parking pattern for a ferry passenger: Early
departure, all-day parking, return early evening. How can parking
management strategies allow recreational boating for guests and crew, but
discourage ferry passengers? Remember that berth revenues are about
2/3 of marina fund revenues. It's important not to institute policies that
render the Berkeley Marina less desirable for boat owners.

Latent Demand: The parking analysis, for EIR purposes, must take into
account unmeasured parking demand created by a new recreational pier,
the reopening of Hs. Lordships as a new restaurant, and the reopening of
the East Dock in the South Cover. These additional parking demands
should be part of the baseline used to assess new impacts of the ferry
service.

Alternatives: Substantive alternatives need to be considered in the EIR
process. Public input to date was only allowed to consider one location,
one ferry operating authority, and one level of service. The only choices
available were the shape and configuration of the breakwater (see "deck
chairs on the Titanic") - and the configuration chosen was based only on
prevailing west-southwest wind and waves with no consideration for
southerly storms or northerly gales. The breakwater design needs to be
vetted by a coastal engineer willing to put their engineering license stamp
on the calculations. Costs will go up. Alternatives need to include alternate
locations, e.g. inside the Berkeley Marina (using part of the current
Hornblower docks), foot of Gilman street, the now-closed racetrack in
Berkeley and Albany, Emeryville Marina, etc. Also alternative levels of
service. Could the ferry be viable with only four departures every weekday
morning, at, say, 150 passengers per departure? (as currently on order)
Does the pricing have to be so highly subsidized, as per the current 22%
farebox recovery? Perhaps a "boutique" ferry that requires much less
subsidy and serves fewer passengers would be a fetter fit for the Berkeley
waterfront.

BCDC constraints: The landfill intended for ferry parking was done under
a BCDC license that dedicates the fill for recreational purpose, and a
project that usurps spaces intended for recreational activities is not allowed
under the permit. City staff seem to believe that Hs. Lordships restaurant,
not strictly a recreational facility, shows that this is not a strict requirement.
However the land is also subject to the California Land Trust restrictions of
1913 (as amended in 1962) and these documents specifically call out
restaurants, golf courses and even airports (I landed at the marina in a
helicopter from SFO '73) as allowable uses. The land grant trust does NOT
include parking for a transit hub or a ferry terminal.

Measure L: Berkeley's measure L creates a statutory requirement that any
significant development on the waterfront is subject to a city-wide
referendum. If a marina-wide parking fee is a necessary part of the ferry
project, this needs to be clear in the wording of the ballot measure.

Economic feasibility: The Marina Fund is underwater. The City is facing a
large budget deficit, as is the State. Federal help seems unlikely in the
current climate. WETA does not have the funds to run the Berkeley service,
as proposed, without additional outside funding. The source and amount
need to be identified in the EIR to determine feasibility. If the project
collapses due to financial infeasibility, then the benefits that might possibly
justify some level of environmental, social and economic impacts will
disappear. A binding update to the MOU between WETA and the City,
stipulating up-front and ongoing costs to the City, is necessary for the EIR
to assess viability.

Compliance with existing plan: The Waterfront Specific Plan (WSP)
revision is incomplete. The current plan does not provide for a ferry
terminal. The plan needs to be updated before the EIR can assess
compliance.

Equity? From the meeting packet for the May WETA Board meeting,
WETA transports 2,595100 one-way passengers per year. Operating costs
are budgeted at $74,748,838 per year. "Repair and replacement" (not
including capitalization for new routes and additions to the fleet) add
another $26,057,363 per years. Do the math. The PUBLIC cost of each
one-way ferry ride is $38.84. For a round trip commute, assuming the fare
is $10 each way, this is like giving each commuter a check for $57.68 every
day. Surveys suggest that about 90% of ferry commuters earn above
median East Bay income. This is not equity. If we have that kind of money
to throw at transportation, let's give more buss passes to high school
students (for example).

Is the project being honestly represented to the public?

The title of "Pier-Ferry Project" implies that reconstructing 500 feet of
recreational pier is a major goal of the project, with something approaching
parity in terms of the project's priorities.

After extensive analysis, the City's parking consultants determined that 389
parking spaces for ferry passengers will be required, and goes to some
lengths to explain how these additional parked cars will not significantly
affect recreational access to the waterfront. How many parking spaces will
be required to serve recreational pier visitors? ZERO, according to the
Kittelson parking studies. See the problem here?

Also, the "E" for "Emergency" reduces the credibility of the WETA meme,
especially when considered along with electrification. A true emergency
ferry system would use vehicle-carrying ferries, capable of transporting
ambulances and fire trucks across the Bay. This could save lives in the first
few hours after a disaster event. Passenger-only ferries address the
inconvenience of being stuck on the wrong side of the Bay, but do little to
protect life and limb.

True emergency ferries need to be agile and versatile enough to load
emergency vehicles from any accessible boat ramp - we don't know which
terminals or ramps will be cut off due to liquefaction or downed
infrastructure.

And finally, electric ferries for emergencies? The shore power grid is likely
to be interrupted, and electric ferries need to recharge during dwell time at
the terminals. The work-around is fixed diesel-generators and batteries at
the terminals, but that essentially doubles the cost of the prime movers.

From Agenda Item 9, Weta Board meeting: December 9, 2021 . " an all-
electric ferry fleet may be cited as a milestone for incentivizing a community
to come out and support the development of a new ferry terminal. "

Without an enforceable statutory requirement for electric ferries on new
routes, this reads like a disingenuous bait-and-switch promise designed to
calm the opposition.

The scope of the El R needs to include a rigorous review of WETA's actual
commitment to electrification at scale. The EIR also needs to evaluate the
efficacy of the ferry system in response to a major earthquake, fire, or
widespread infrastructure failure. Would it be more honest to drop the "E?"

Hello Liza,

San Francisco Bay is one of the best open water swimming locations in the world and the Berkeley Marina is a very
popular location to enjoy this sport. I want to encourage the City of Berkeley to keep the needs of open water
swimmers in mind when reviewing the plan to bring a Ferry to the Berkeley pier area.
                                                                 1
I have been swimming in the bay for over 10 years, and many others for longer than that. I've seen the sport grow in
popularity here over the years, and it is a sport that is growing worldwide. The Seine river in Paris recently opened to
open water swimming to help meet this demand.

San Francisco Bay is an especially good venue for open water swimming, as it has swimmable weather and water
temperatures year round. People use SF bay to train for swimming the English Channel and other challenging
swims. And the cove to the right of Hs Lordship's is unique in the east bay as it has sufficient water depth to swim even
at the lowest tides. Swimmers value this location, and it is sometimes their only option when the tide is too low to swim
at Crown Beach, Albany Beach, Keller Beach or the Berkeley Sailing Basin.

Open water swimmers do not need a lot of resources. We need a place to park, a place to safely enter and exit the
water, and a swim area relatively free of fast watercraft. And although not strictly needed, a shower to rinse off after is
nice.

Could the City of Berkeley please consider the needs of open water swimmers when reviewing this project?
1) Please ensure we have space to park our cars. We commonly park for 1-2 hours at a time, but we swim in groups for
safety. We might use a few to a dozen or so spaces at any one time. Groups go out at different times during the day,
some before work at first light, some after work when there is light, some at lunch hour, and some in between. We
currently share this parking with fishermen, kayakers, dog walkers, picnickers and people just enjoying the view from
their cars. If these spaces are all taken by commuters, it will eliminate this spot as a viable swim location. Could you
ensure that there are spaces with an appropriate time limit to accommodate the existing and projected users, to
preserve this area for us swimmers and other recreational users?
2) Please ensure that there is open water set aside for swimmers (the bay is huge, we are small). We don't mind sharing
with kayakers and small sailboats, but ferries and fast moving craft are a real danger for us. We commonly swim out to
the break in the pier and back from Hs Lordships, but we can adjust that if a Ferry needs some of that water,
too. Maybe some buoys could separate a swim zone from a ferry zone?
3) Please ensure we have a safe spot to enter and exit the water. A beach is the best, but a protected gravel path to
below the low tide point as exists at Hs Lordships works. A dock with a ladder also works if it is not crowded
with fishermen and their fish hooks.
4) And as long as improvements are being considered, could we get a shower to rinse off?

Thank you,

Paul Young

Re: Scope of Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry

Dear Ms. McNulty and staff of the San Francisco Bay Area Water Emergency Transportation
Authority (WETA):

This comment addresses environmental impacts involving “Hazards and Hazardous Materials”
that the Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry must
address. I write as a long-time resident of Berkeley and general supporter of the ferry system, not
representing any group.

The project creates hazard well beyond simple negligence, because all traffic in or out must thread
through a single, narrow, half-mile bottleneck, with no alternative or emergency route. This could
trap large numbers of people. It also could cut off a substantial portion of Berkeley’s police vehicle
fleet , crippling emergency responses.

The project as out lined is expected to draw large and increasing numbers of people and vehicles, at
earlier and later hours than now, to a peninsula
    • Jutting a half mile into the Bay
    • Built of unconsolidated fill supported by rip-rap
    • Subject to well documented tsunami and earthquake hazard
    • In the face of sea-level rise reasonably likely to reach 5’ by 2100 (the standard the East Bay
         Regional Park District is using for the North Basin Strip and Virginia Extension just north).
    • with only one exit or access route: low-lying University Avenue.

This is reckless. The project could easily work against its stated objective “Provide options for
emergency response and transportation services in case of an emergency, such as natural or
human-caused event that disables roads, other transit, bridges, and/or tunnels.” Significant
numbers of people in new hotels, restaurants, and other commercial activities envisioned, as well
as ferry users and those using the area’s parks now, could easily be trapped, injured, or killed. The
ferry, too small for crowds or emergency vehicles, could not help them.

This danger must be considered in terms of both immediate impacts of the pier and ferry and
cumulative impacts of t he City of Berkeley's Waterfront Specific Plan (WSP). The WSP
envisions commercial redevelopment of the Marina area with multiple hotels and restaurants. It
was begun in conjunction with the ferry/pier plan and is being prepared in tandem, with approval
hoped for in 2026. The WSP relies on the ferry as a draw -- Meetings and presentations made clear

Schwartz, comments on EIR Scope for Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry             1
that the existing hotel struggles due to distance from other Berkeley centers of interest; the ferry
may attract San Francisco visitors looking for lower-cost accommodation. B ringing significantly
more people to this vulnerable spot at late hours and overnight will make escape more
confusing and difficult. .

University Avenue now backs up and moves at a crawl when public events draw heavy traffic.
In an earthquake, tsunami warning (such as recently occurred), or actual tsunami, drivers trying to
escape would likely cross the medians into oncoming lanes, blocking emergency vehicles. An
earthquake that ruptures pavement or creates a sink, or a single stall or wreck, could
compound disaster. Since much of Berkeley's police fleet is kept at the Marina, it might not be
able to get out or even by reached.

As sea-level rise and climate change continue, risk will increase. The strip of land south of
University is eroding rapidly in several areas. Wind and storm already wash large logs and wrack
to the base of the low rise to the Bay Trail spur and University Avenue (see photo below and link
above). Large, windy, rainy storms are increasing due to climate change. The resulting high tides
and effective sea-level rise, often called storm surge, will in the foreseeable future wash spray or
even waves onto trail and road.

https://chavezpark.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Jim-McGrath-on-parking-Additions-to-comments.pdf

Related and separate to the above note: We now hear that the Doubletree Hotel, one of if not the
biggest revenue source for the Marina, is close to foreclosure and not paying its agreed amount to
Berkeley. Parks Director Scott Ferris made the statement that hotels all over the bay area are suffering,
and he even said something to the effect that people aren't wanting to come to the bay area or so it
sounded like to me. I have a recording of that. Yet only recently the same people now proposing this
ferry/pier project were asking us to envision more hotel rooms or another hotel! I believe their vision for
"food courts" and "food trucks" are equally short-sighted. I understand Berkeley needs money, but it can't
be at the expense of the health of its community members! Please consider this honestly and fully.

ALSO, MONEYMAKING IDEA:, The Doubletree DOES have the potential for a lovely restaurant with a
view of the bay right now. However, at $30 for parking, I assume many choose to park along Marina
Boulevard while the hotel parking lot is mostly empty. Can some jiggling around be done about this? One
reason more people DON'T love the restaurant at this hotel (other than the unnecessarily loud
overhead music) is that very large boats are now allowed to park right in front of the restaurnt
window and block view of the bay. If Berkeley needs money, how about making a different
arrangement for docking those large tour boats? I understand Berkeley in fact paid money for the
pier at which they're docked! A mistake, unless that pier can be used instead for some sensible-
sized boats and the eyesore tour boats moved farther west in the bay.

6.1. Climate Risk Summary
Cal-Adapt midcentury 2040–2059 average projections for four hazards are reported below for your project location. These are under Representation Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5 which
assumes GHG emissions will continue to rise strongly through 2050 and then plateau around 2100.
Climate Hazard                                                    Result for Project Location                                       Unit

Temperature and Extreme Heat                                      7.10000                                                           annual days of extreme heat

Extreme Precipitation                                             7.50000                                                           annual days with precipitation above 20 mm

Sea Level Rise                                                    —                                                                 meters of inundation depth

Wildfire                                                          0.00000                                                           annual hectares burned


Temperature and Extreme Heat data are for grid cell in which your project are located. The projection is based on the 98th historical percentile of daily maximum/minimum temperatures from
observed historical data (32 climate model ensemble from Cal-Adapt, 2040–2059 average under RCP 8.5). Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.
Extreme Precipitation data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The threshold of 20 mm is equivalent to about ¾ an inch of rain, which would be light to moderate rainfall if
received over a full day or heavy rain if received over a period of 2 to 4 hours. Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.



                                                                                                40 / 49
                                                                                                                Berkeley WTPF Project - Operations Detailed Report, 1/16/2026


Sea Level Rise data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The projections are from Radke et al. (2017), as reported in Cal-Adapt (Radke et al., 2017, CEC-500-2017-008), and
consider inundation location and depth for the San Francisco Bay, the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta and California coast resulting different increments of sea level rise coupled with
extreme storm events. Users may select from four scenarios to view the range in potential inundation depth for the grid cell. The four scenarios are: No rise, 0.5 meter, 1.0 meter, 1.41 meters
Wildfire data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The projections are from UC Davis, as reported in Cal-Adapt (2040–2059 average under RCP 8.5), and consider historical data
of climate, vegetation, population density, and large (> 400 ha) fire history. Users may select from four model simulations to view the range in potential wildfire probabilities for the grid cell. The
four simulations make different assumptions about expected rainfall and temperature are: Warmer/drier (HadGEM2-ES), Cooler/wetter (CNRM-CM5), Average conditions (CanESM2), Range of
different rainfall and temperature possibilities (MIROC5). Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.
